quote.text: intervening in the male⇒female direction raises the logit for choosing “queen” over “king” as the next word, but does not change the logit for “King” over “king”

items.technical: Counterfactual-pair differences give directions for morphology, translation and category hierarchy that act as linear probes and interventions, especially under a causal or head-derived inner product, and LDA directions steer tense and aspect.
items.why: Solid by the literature rule. 9 papers in the family report it, 2 with held-out accuracy (rubric B yes) and 6 with a measured intervention (rubric C yes), over 7 open model families (BERT-family, CLIP/ViT, Falcon, Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Qwen). P1074 argues plain vector arithmetic is weak in modern sentence embeddings and uses rotations, a qualified limit.
items.note: Raw hidden states support this less well than transformed spaces, 47 against 80 percent in P3313, which is the same lesson as our whitening. P1108 (2026) adds that attribute directions with thresholds form WordNet concept lattices, though its train and test split is not stated.

items.title: Context moves where a statement sits on the truth line
items.line: Instructions to lie, social pressure, a user profile or a long conversation shift how the model internally rates the same fact.
items.status: 6 papers, 4 with a measured intervention, 5 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: Dead or alive probe accuracy under role-play against without it, Llama

quote.text: Deceptive instructions induce significant representational shifts compared to Truthful/Neutral representations (which are similar), concentrated in early-to-mid layers

items.technical: The projection of a fixed statement on a truth or belief direction shifts with context, under deceptive instructions (concentrated in early-to-mid layers), multi-turn pressure (hidden states drift toward a learnable flip boundary), added context (larger truth-vector changes when it conflicts with parametric knowledge), personalisation and conversation history.
items.why: Solid because 6 papers report it, 5 with held-out accuracy (B yes) and 4 with a measured intervention (C yes), across 4 coded model families (Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Qwen). No paper in the family reports a truth reading unaffected by these contexts.
items.note: P0624 also finds the instructed True or False output stays predictable by linear probes across conditions (lines 18-20), so the shift moves the readout rather than destroying it. The strongest case, a truth probe reading relevant facts backwards late in a conversation, rests on P2305 alone and is kept as a separate new finding.

items.title: Syntax trees, parse states and bindings are readable and causal
items.line: Probes read dependency types, unfinished parses, entity bindings and bracket depth, and editing those directions changes what the model predicts.
items.status: 8 papers, 5 with a measured intervention, 4 with held-out accuracy, 3 against

quote.text: On average across dependency types, the Polar Probe reaches a AUC score of 95%

items.technical: Polar probes recover dependency types at 95 percent AUC, gradient edits of parse-state probes shift ambiguous continuations about eightfold, binding-index subspaces steer relational answers, and ablating a stack-depth direction collapses accuracy.
items.why: Solid by the literature rule, with one flagged call. 8 papers in the family report it, 4 with held-out accuracy (rubric B yes) and 5 with a measured intervention (rubric C yes), over 8 open model families (BERT-family, GPT-2, Gemma, Llama, Mistral, OLMo, Pythia/GPT-NeoX, Qwen). P0224, P0683 and P3109 state their limits. P0587 reads scenario element and argument pairs below 0.5 and does not qualify it, which we judge a different quantity from binding subspaces.
items.note: P0224 finds the binding subspace moves between discourse contexts and needs a translation vector, and P0683 finds no single direction for ambiguity. P3361 works on toy counter languages and P0343 on an LSTM. P3109 finds function vectors form for negation cues but barely steer negation scope. P0587 probes a concatenation of two hidden states, which its coder flagged as stretching the direction definition. If that result is counted as the same kind of binding, the binding part of this finding is shaky rather than solid. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0224).

items.title: Stated confidence and actual correctness sit on different directions
items.line: How sure the model sounds and whether it is right are carried by different internal signals, so steering one need not fix the other.
items.status: 5 papers, 5 with a measured intervention, 4 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: Cosine between the correctness probe and the abstention decision probe

quote.text: Pure incorrectness features are functionally inert

items.technical: Directions or SAE features for verbal or output confidence are nearly orthogonal to or dissociable from correctness directions, and steering the confidence direction shifts hedging or abstention without tracking correctness.
items.why: Solid because 5 papers report it, 4 with held-out accuracy (B yes) and 5 with a measured intervention (C yes), the coded model families of these papers span 5 families (DeepSeek, Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Qwen), and no paper in the family shows it failing.
items.note: Most support is from 2026 (P0753, P1733, P2244, P2563), with P0561 (2025) the earliest. P1733 also finds confounded features that carry both signals, so the two are not fully separate everywhere. P0561 compares verbal uncertainty with semantic uncertainty, a proxy for correctness rather than correctness itself.

items.title: Harm arrows still rank scary but harmless prompts correctly
items.line: Prompts that sound harmful but are harmless still score below real harmful ones, though above ordinary harmless prompts.
items.status: registered, the expected falsifier fired

numbers.label: XSTest whole-set AUROC, three directions
OR-Bench whole-set AUROC, three directions
lowest OR-Bench category
share of benign-looking prompts above the median benign item
whole-set rankings
lowest category
share of look-alike prompts above the median harmful item, P0334 direction, XSTest and OR-Bench

quote.text: pseudo-harmful instructions overlap with harmful features, causing over-harmful encoding

items.technical: Under refusal-category, harmful-query and harmfulness directions, XSTest and OR-Bench harmless-but-scary prompts are ranked against harmful ones at AUROC 0.918 to 0.995 as whole sets and 0.838 or more per category, so the registered attempt to build a misread group found nothing to flip, yet 0.872 to 1.000 of them score above the median ordinary benign item. This matches reports that pseudo-harmful prompts overlap harmful features (P1087) and that an AdvBench probe reads harm rather than scary surface, though at a lower AUC of 0.79 (P1799).
items.why: Solid. Our registered construction test (RUNLOG lines 12445 to 12502) predicted flips and its falsifier fired on all three directions, a clean outcome that matched the stated expectation, and two family papers report the same pattern.
items.note: At a deployed threshold many of these prompts may still be flagged. RUNLOG says none scores above the median harmful item, but flip_p0334.json gives 0.004 on XSTest and 0.018 on OR-Bench, so that wording is slightly off. Two of the three directions come from papers outside this reading (P1475, P0334), and the third is P3218. Merged from 2 verified findings across refusal-safety (rste19, rmon09).

items.title: Probes read many finer word and sentence properties
items.line: Held-out probes read word boundaries, verb types, tense, number, sentence complexity, dialect and sensory wording, though some reads need a control.
items.status: 6 papers, 1 with a measured intervention, 6 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: Phrasal against prepositional verb probe accuracy, BERT layer 6 (logistic regression)
Best sensory probe fit, concreteness, deeper layers

quote.text: linear probes to identify that these models implicitly track word boundaries, even when they do not appear in training

items.technical: Linear probes on frozen hidden states recover word-boundary position across 31 languages, phrasal against prepositional verbs, grammatical number and tense, context complexity, Arabic dialect and part of speech, and most sensory axes on held-out items, while untrained-model baselines and cluster separability tests show part of the accuracy can come from the probe or the data.
items.why: Solid by the literature rule. 6 papers in the family report it, 6 with held-out accuracy (rubric B yes) and 1 with a measured intervention (rubric C yes), over 9 open model families (BERT-family, GPT-2, Gemma, Llama, OLMo, Phi, Pythia/GPT-NeoX, Qwen, T5). The caveats (untrained baselines in P3196, weak cluster separability in P3050, MSA models missing dialect nuance in P3005) are stated by the authors.
items.note: These are readouts, not uses. Only P0689 intervenes, and on its SAE features rather than the complexity probe. P3196 shows why a control matters, since balanced probes on untrained models reach 68% from phoneme position statistics alone. Deeper semantic relations are less readable, see P0587 in the finding on syntax and bindings.

items.title: Safety directions make VLMs refuse more harmful image requests
items.line: Adding a safety or shift-correcting direction at inference cuts attack success on most multimodal safety benchmarks tested, and suppressing it raises attack success.
items.status: 5 papers, 5 with a measured intervention, 3 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: P0684 LLaVA-7B unsafe rate on multimodal input, before and after

quote.text: the unsafe rate of LLaVA-7B on multi-modal input can be reduced from 61.53% to as low as 3.15% with only inference-time intervention.

items.technical: Difference-of-means, probe-weight and PCA shift directions added at inference lower VLM attack success or unsafe rates on most benchmarks tested (LLaVA-7B unsafe rate 61.53 to 3.15 percent in P0684, average attack-success reductions of 34.34 to 52.98 percent on four benchmarks in P0036, near-zero attack success on several benchmarks in P2845 and P0556), and suppressing the probed safety circuit raises attack success (P1248), so the direction is causal for refusal.
items.why: Solid for the scoped claim. 5 papers with C yes (B yes in P0036, P0556, P1248), across LLaVA (Llama family), Qwen-VL, Gemma 3, InternVL and Chameleon. The failures are on single subsets, P0556 qualifies its Chameleon image-only case, and P2845 leaves one HoliSafe subset largely unrefused, which does not contradict a claim limited to most benchmarks and is carried in the finding on generality claims.
items.note: P2845 and P0556 are in both lists because they report the effect and show where it stops. P1248 uses the direction to attack, not defend. P0036 and P2845 choose layer and strength on evaluation data (our layer coding swept-test). It is unclear whether P0036 reports percentage points or relative reductions. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0556, P2845).

items.title: Personality trait vectors turn traits up or down gradually
items.line: Directions for Big Five traits such as extraversion or agreeableness let a user raise or lower a trait step by step.
items.status: 8 papers, 8 with a measured intervention, 3 against

numbers.label: PersonalityBench mean score, vector algebra against fine-tuning upper bound

quote.text: we observe a monotonic relationship between the steering coefficient α and the magnitude of the expressed personality trait.

items.technical: Contrastive high-minus-low trait directions for the Big Five and similar persona traits, scaled by a coefficient, produce graded and often monotone or sigmoidal changes in judged trait expression on questionnaires and free generation, on Llama, Qwen, Mistral and Gemma models.
items.why: Solid. 8 papers show it with measured interventions (rubric C yes) on Llama, Qwen, Mistral and Gemma, and the papers with traits that do not move (P2702 on narcissism, P0165 in its personality domain) state the limit themselves.
items.note: No support paper reports held-out accuracy (rubric B yes) for the trait direction itself, so the evidence is steering outcomes scored by an LLM judge or a questionnaire. P0165 reports limited effectiveness in its personality domain and names it an open problem. Control is often sigmoidal rather than linear in the coefficient (P1234, P1336). P1336 moved to against, since it is a theory paper that reports non-monotonic effects of steering strength rather than graded trait control. P2702 added to against for narcissism, a dark-triad trait rather than a Big Five one.

items.title: Training on many datasets gives a more general truth direction
items.line: A truth reader trained on a wide mix of datasets works on new datasets far better than one trained on a single dataset.
items.status: 5 papers, 4 with a measured intervention, 5 with held-out accuracy, 2 against

numbers.label: Single-dataset against joint training, cross-domain AUC

quote.text: increasing the diversity of the training datasets significantly enhances the performance in all scenarios

items.technical: Probes fitted jointly on many truth datasets or domains generalise across held-out tasks and domains where single-dataset probes transfer near randomly, for example joint multi-dataset training restoring 0.73 to 0.91 AUC where single-dataset probes give 0.39 to 0.66 in P3560.
items.why: Solid because 5 papers report it, 5 with held-out accuracy (B yes) and 4 with a measured intervention (C yes), across 6 coded model families (GPT-2, Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Pythia/GPT-NeoX, Qwen). P3104 (deception domains grow more specific with scale) and P3306 (common probes give no transferable veracity direction) limit it, but neither tests joint training on the target mix, so they bound rather than refute it.
items.note: P0192 is left out of support because its cross-domain gain comes from a guiding prompt rather than more varied training data. P3214 gets its gain from mixing contexts on synthetic capability data. The joint direction still has to include data like the target, so this is not evidence of one universal truth direction.

items.title: Unsafe fine-tuning drift is visible along a direction
items.line: When fine-tuning makes a model broadly misaligned, the change shows up along an internal direction a cheap monitor can track.
items.status: 6 papers, 6 with a measured intervention

numbers.label: P2841 held-out AUROC
supporting papers coded C yes and B yes
numbers.value: 6 of 6 C yes, 0 of 6 B yes
numbers.where: codes.C.mark and codes.B.mark over the 6 support ids

quote.text: A low-overhead monitor built on this drift profile detects dangerous checkpoints with 2.2% false negative rate, 2.9% false positive rate, and 0.990 AUROC on held-out perturbation types

items.technical: Emergent misalignment and safety drift during fine-tuning or reinforcement learning appear as movement along a low-dimensional activation direction, and steering along that direction changes the misaligned behaviour. Held-out detection of affected checkpoints is reported by P2841 only.
items.why: Six papers, all coded C yes in papers.json, over Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, Phi and DeepSeek among open families. None is coded B yes, so the held-out detection part rests on P2841 alone and is not part of the solid claim.
items.note: P2841 says deployment across very different training regimes may need recalibration. P1696's cross-model transfer of such directions fails its specificity controls, so the direction is per model. P0125 is outside the 149-paper selection. A model trained on purpose to hide from monitors is a separate case, see the evasion finding.

items.title: Who goes with what sits in a small subspace
items.line: Which entity goes with which attribute is held in a small set of directions, and editing those directions swaps the pairing the model reports.
items.status: 5 papers, 5 with a measured intervention, 3 with held-out accuracy, 1 against

quote.text: We discover that LMs encode (or store) the OI information into a low-rank subspace (called OI subspace hereafter), and the discovered OI subspace can causally affect binding behaviour and thus BI information as well.

items.technical: Binding-ID difference vectors, ordering-ID principal components, a Hessian-derived binding subspace, an additive entity-relation address and a 3D list-indexing channel mediate entity-attribute binding, and patching or steering along them swaps which attribute the model retrieves.
items.why: Solid. At least 3 papers with C yes, at least 2 families, and no paper shows binding directions failing to mediate binding within a task, and the one method caution (P3705) is qualified by its authors. Counts. 5 supporting papers, 3 with rubric B yes, 5 with rubric C yes, 4 open model families (API-only families not counted), 1 from 2026, 1 against or limiting.
items.note: Existence and causal use hold in every paper. Transfer of binding vectors across tasks is uneven (P0913 BIOS-derived vector reads CAPITALS at 0.47 with chance 0.33) and propositional probes drop on translated inputs (P0988), both taken up in the transfer and weak-group findings. P3334 is a 2-layer toy model. P3705, a recall addition outside this family, shows that subspace patching can change outputs through a dormant pathway, so a patching effect alone does not prove the subspace is the one the model uses. Its authors say this does not make subspace patching unfit.

items.title: Topic arrows make the model write about a chosen subject
items.line: Adding an arrow for a topic such as football or church makes more replies about it, and grafting concept activity does the same.
items.status: 5 papers, 5 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: Distractor refusal accuracy with the topic steering vector, Llama, best setting (gain over no steering)

quote.text: The user-selected λ-feature strength modulates prevalence of the target feature, though the exact relationship between feature strength and λ can vary between concepts.

items.technical: Difference-of-means concept vectors for OneSeC topics under closed-loop control, topic-maintenance steering vectors, grafted population-average concept chunks and dense SAE latent pairs raise judged concept prevalence or topic adherence in generation, with a dose response that varies by concept.
items.why: Solid by the literature rule. 5 papers in the family report it, 1 with held-out accuracy (rubric B yes) and 5 with a measured intervention (rubric C yes), over 8 open model families (BERT-family, CLIP/ViT, GPT-2, Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Qwen, T5). The limit in P1508 is stated by its authors.
items.note: Prevalence is judged by an LLM in P1283 and P1508. P1508 finds that dense latent pairs steer toward the concept in context, but unclear judgments rise sharply on out-of-context examples. P0858 compares static topic vectors with a learned module in a vision-language model, but its topic table is garbled in our text, so it is not counted. The benchmark comparison with prompting is in the finding on steering costs. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P1508).

items.title: Sparse autoencoder features change when retrained
items.line: Retraining a sparse dictionary with a new seed, new data or pruning gives a partly different set of features.
items.status: 7 papers, 4 with a measured intervention, 3 with held-out accuracy, 3 against

numbers.label: our own split-half reliability, difference of means (pairs kept) and converged logistic probe
numbers.value: own split-half reliability 0.966 for the difference of means with minimal pairs kept together (A09); 0.596 for the probe and 0.948 for the component, still with the pair-splitting code

quote.text: only 30% of the features were shared across different seeds

items.technical: SAEs trained on the same model and data with different seeds share only about 30 percent of features in a 131K-latent SAE on Llama 3 8B (P1097), stability across seeds depends on the SAE's training data (P3035) and ensembling is proposed to raise it (P1254). For optimised vectors the corpus disagrees, since steering vectors fit five times on one prompt converge to different directions (P0816) while latent task vectors trained five times per task show strong intra-task alignment (P1105).
items.why: The SAE part is reported by 3 papers (P1097, P3035, P1254), with B yes in P3035 and P1254 (both C no in papers.json), over GPT-2, Gemma, Llama and Pythia, and no corpus paper was found showing seed-invariant SAE features without qualification. The optimised-vector part is contested (P0816 against P1105), so it is carried as a limit rather than as part of the solid claim.
items.note: Our probe reliability still uses the older pair-splitting code (factsheet.json estimators-and-sae), so it is indicative only. Part of the open problem that the estimated direction is not a unique, stable object (100 papers, open_problems.json synth.problems[5]). Merged from 2 verified findings across cross-cutting, other (prac10, othe27). The family readers placed these under problematic, solid; the editor placed the merged item under solid.

items.title: Different harm categories share nearly one direction
items.line: Weapons, hate, scams and other kinds of harm line up along almost the same arrow, so one arrow covers them.
items.status: 5 papers, 5 with a measured intervention, 2 with held-out accuracy, 1 against

numbers.label: agreement of group directions, Refusal harm categories (arditi_cat)
agreement of group directions, Harmfulness 55 subconcepts
agreement of group directions, Harmfulness harm categories
agreement and lowest held-out group, Harmful queries categories (P0334) and India-specific harms (P3086)
numbers.where: sets['Harmful queries, categories'] and sets['India-specific harms, categories'], rho and loso_min

quote.text: the classifier vectors from all but the second-to-last layer of the model have effective rank K = 1

items.technical: Directions fitted per harm category or subconcept are close to collinear (effective rank 1 over 55 probe directions in P3218), one harmful vector improves every SafeEdit category (P1470), a neuron ablation acts uniformly across four HarmBench categories though a suicide circuit is partly separate (P2477), content-policy refusal splits cluster together (P2800), and our re-reading of four harm-category datasets (five readings, two of which share one dataset) finds group agreement of 0.756 to 0.957 with every category read at 0.980 or better when held out.
items.why: Solid. Five family papers report it, with held-out accuracy in P3218 and P2477 and measured interventions in all five, over Llama, Qwen, Gemma and Mistral, and our datasets agree. P1087 finds non-collinear directions only for harmless-but-scary categories, a different contrast, P3324 reports shared but asymmetric structure, and P2477 names its suicide circuit as partly distinct, all kept as stated limits.
items.note: Our harm-categories and 55-subconcepts datasets share the same activations and labels (factsheet claim corpus-protocol), so they are one dataset, not two. P3324 is listed both ways because its categories share representations but interventions spread between them unevenly. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P2477, P3324).

items.title: Steering along a harm direction changes what agents do
items.line: Adding or removing a harm or refusal direction inside an agent's model raises or cuts its harmful actions by large margins.
items.status: 4 papers, 4 with a measured intervention, 2 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: P1713 coding-agent attack success, vanilla vs AgentLens, LLaMA-3.1-8B
P0125 refusal rate on harmful WebDojo tasks, fine-tuned agent before and after steering
P0395 attack success after subtracting the refusal direction

quote.text: On LLaMA-3.1-8B, it reduces ASR from 73.80% under the vanilla agent to 16.70%

items.technical: Steering along probe-derived harm or refusal directions changes agent behaviour, cutting coding-agent attack success from 73.80 to 16.70 percent on LLaMA-3.1-8B (P1713), raising a fine-tuned web agent's refusal of harmful tasks from 0 to 95.9 percent (P0125), raising deep-research attack success from 8 to 32 percent when the refusal direction is subtracted (P0395), and controlling search-query safety in agentic RL, where a projection penalty restores alignment (P3335).
items.why: Solid. 4 papers with C yes (B yes in P1713 and P0395), over Llama, Qwen and QwQ backbones per papers.json model_families, and we found no paper in the corpus showing such steering fail on agent harm.
items.note: All four are 2026 papers, and P1713 and P3335 are a preprint and a workshop paper. P0125 is coded refusal only, so outside the family by concept code. P1713 and P3335 pick layers on evaluation data and P0395 uses the final layer with no stated reason (our layer coding). P2418 reports that static CAA and Mass-Mean vectors struggle for procedural agent skills (P2418.txt lines 430-431), so this finding is about harm and refusal, not task success.

items.title: Being tested versus deployed is a readable direction
items.line: Models hold a readable sense of being tested rather than deployed, and two papers turn it up or down by steering.
items.status: 4 papers, 3 with a measured intervention, 3 with held-out accuracy

quote.text: Steering toward unawareness reduces it to 0.81% and 0.00%, respectively; steering toward awareness raises it to 57.9% and 54.7%.

items.technical: Probe and mean-difference directions separate evaluation from deployment contexts with high held-out accuracy, and steering along them raises or suppresses verbalised evaluation awareness and evaluation-specific behaviour, even when the vector is built on the model before the behaviour was trained in.
items.why: Solid for representation. Steering is shown by two papers only. At least 3 papers with B or C yes over at least 2 families, and no paper shows it failing. Counts. 4 supporting papers, 3 with rubric B yes, 3 with rubric C yes, 5 open model families (API-only families not counted), 1 from 2026, 0 against or limiting.
items.note: What awareness does to safety is unsettled. P1593 finds the effect on harmful compliance and stereotypes varies in size and sign across models, and the P3237 power law of awareness with model size uses each model’s best layer by AUROC on the evaluation set (lt_coding swept-test), so that part is shaky. Only P1593 and P3291 steer along the awareness direction. P3237 and P0400 only read it, and P0400 coded C yes for its shortcut direction, not this one. P0400 also finds the awareness direction engages inconsistently across its two models during RL training.

items.title: Quality judgments read from inside can beat the model’s verdict
items.line: A read-out of the inside can score essays, answers and research ideas well, sometimes better than asking the same model for its verdict.
items.status: 5 papers, 1 with a measured intervention, 4 with held-out accuracy

quote.text: small LMs, despite with weak generative ability, encode rich evaluative signals in their hidden states.

items.technical: PCA and probe directions on hidden states score text quality, reasoning-answer aspects, research-idea novelty, essay traits and learned feedback, correlating with human judgments across held-out datasets and beating prompted judgments from the same small models.
items.why: Solid. At least 3 papers with B yes over at least 2 families, and the limits are stated by the papers themselves. Counts. 5 supporting papers, 4 with rubric B yes, 1 with rubric C yes, 7 open model families (API-only families not counted), 3 from 2026, 2 against or limiting.
items.note: P1092 restricts its out-of-distribution claim to binary judgments because multiclass transfer is near chance. P0049 picks the best head on the test prompt and says the baseline comparison therefore does not show it wins. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0049, P1092).

items.title: Language arrows overlap early and group by family
items.line: Arrows for different languages point much the same way in early layers and drift apart later, and related languages sit closest.
items.status: 6 papers, 6 with a measured intervention, 1 against

numbers.label: Agreement of per-language directions, Parallel sentences (P0407 data), our reading
Agreement of per-language directions, Translated sentences (P1897 data), our reading

quote.text: Our language steers capture, to some extent, language families

items.technical: Per-language steering or mean directions show high pairwise cosine, strongest at early layers, and cluster or form simplices by language family under Euclidean or causal inner products.
items.why: Solid by the literature rule. 6 papers in the family report it, 0 with held-out accuracy (rubric B yes) and 6 with a measured intervention (rubric C yes), over 5 open model families (BERT-family, Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Qwen). Our re-measurement agrees, with group directions agreeing at about 0.8 on two independent language datasets.
items.note: P0281 limits this to text in its usual script, since romanized Hindi or Russian lands on almost separate units. Our agreement numbers are from one reading (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, layer 16, last token) on shared-reference datasets where every language is scored against English. Per-language similarity is high early and falls with depth (P1861, P0696).

items.title: A direction can switch between trusting image and prior
items.line: A single contrast direction can push a VLM to answer from the image or from memorised knowledge, flipping most colour answers.
items.status: 4 papers, 4 with a measured intervention, 2 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: P0592 predictions shifted from prior to counterfactual

quote.text: On average, PvP successfully shifts 99.3% of color and 80.8% of size predictions from priors to counterfactuals.

items.technical: Difference-of-means vectors contrasting pixel-grounded with knowledge-grounded prompts, or vision-context with text-context instructions, shift VLM answers between visual evidence and priors, flipping 99.3 percent of colour and 80.8 percent of size predictions from prior to counterfactual (P0592), amplifying modality preference toward a chosen side (P1256), improving grounding by 1.4 to 3.8 points at each model's best configuration (P0390), and reducing hallucination through a textual-prior cause vector (P0601).
items.why: Solid. 4 papers with C yes (B yes in P0390 and P0601), across LLaVA-Next, Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, Janus-Pro and InternVL. P0390 limits its own steering result to a proof of actionability that degrades some samples, a qualified limit.
items.note: Our group coding reads P0592 Table 3 as asymmetric, easier toward the image than back to the prior and easier for colour than size, but that reading is marked uncertain. All four papers choose the layer or layer window on the evaluation data (our layer coding swept-test for P0390, P0592, P0601 and P1256), so the reported sizes are optimistic. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0390).

items.title: Game boards and spatial states are readable and editable
items.line: Models trained on games or on spatial text keep the board or the position as directions that probes read and that edits change.
items.status: 4 papers, 3 with a measured intervention, 4 with held-out accuracy

quote.text: We derive a player skill vector and add it to the model, improving the model’s win rate by up to 2.6 times.

items.technical: Linear probes on residual streams decode per-square board state (chess, Othello), player skill, viewpoint and spatial variables on held-out games or items, and adding or editing along probe directions changes moves, win rate or answers, though in natural-language spatial tasks the states are transient and weakly used.
items.why: Solid. At least 3 papers, B and C yes in several, at least 2 families, and the limiting papers qualify their own claims. Counts. 4 supporting papers, 4 with rubric B yes, 3 with rubric C yes, 2 open model families (API-only families not counted), 2 from 2026, 2 against or limiting.
items.note: P0373 and P3010 train small models from scratch on game transcripts, so model-family counts here are loose. P2097 and P0258 limit the claim for text-only spatial reasoning (encoded but weakly bound to the answer), and both say so themselves. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0258, P2097).

items.title: Format, length and verbosity arrows make models follow rules
items.line: An arrow from prompts with and without an instruction makes the model follow format, length or brevity rules even when the instruction is missing.
items.status: 5 papers, 5 with a measured intervention

quote.text: When steering is applied, we observe a consistent increase in instruction adherence across all models, with accuracy improving to approximately 30%.

items.technical: Instruction-difference vectors raise IFEval-style format, length and word-inclusion adherence, verbose-to-concise CoT vectors cut reasoning length and transfer between MATH500 and GSM8K at cosine 0.92, and conciseness vectors compose with language vectors.
items.why: Solid by the literature rule. 5 papers in the family report it, 0 with held-out accuracy (rubric B yes) and 5 with a measured intervention (rubric C yes), over 6 open model families (DeepSeek, Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Phi, Qwen).
items.note: Effects without an explicit instruction stay partial, about 30 percent adherence in P0971.

items.title: Belief states can be read and strengthened by steering
items.line: Models keep track of what a character believes, and adding that direction fixes many wrong belief answers, though less so for action questions.
items.status: 4 papers, 3 with a measured intervention, 2 with held-out accuracy

quote.text: CAA consistently delivers the most substantial accuracy improvements across all models and tasks, up to +56 for Llama-2-13B-chat on the Backward Belief task

items.technical: Logistic probes decode protagonist and oracle belief states above chance in LMs and VLMs, and contrastive activation addition or head-direction steering raises accuracy on true-belief and false-belief questions, while steering belief leaves cooperative action predictions unchanged.
items.why: Solid for belief questions. At least 3 papers with B or C yes over at least 2 families, and the limits concern action questions and prompt changes, not belief questions. Counts. 4 supporting papers, 2 with rubric B yes, 3 with rubric C yes, 7 open model families (API-only families not counted), 2 from 2026, 2 against or limiting.
items.note: P0832 itself calls the belief representations brittle to prompt variations, and its CAA vector moves the held-out Forward Action task much less (see the weak-group finding). P0225 gives only a partial held-out check. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0832, P1811).

items.title: Tool use has a readable and steerable direction
items.line: Whether and how well a model calls a tool can be read from its activations, and one direction can dial tool calling up or down.
items.status: 4 papers, 3 with a measured intervention, 3 with held-out accuracy, 1 against

numbers.label: P1656 pooled over-calling rate before and after gated steering
P2858 open-domain QA accuracy with live tool execution under steering

quote.text: Adding the direction with strength α moves the call rate monotonically from near 0% to over 90% while keeping calls well-formed.

items.technical: Linear probes detect incorrect tool calls at AUROC above 0.80 for most of 18 BFCL models and generalize to unseen error types (P2749), sparse neuron detectors catch over-calling and missing calls at ROC-AUC 0.90 to 1.00 before generation (P1656), a difference-of-means direction moves the tool-call rate monotonically from near 0 to over 90 percent and transfers to unseen tools (P2858), steering along a shared neuron basis cuts over-calling from 0.131 to 0.026 (P1656), and one RL-specific crosscoder feature adds 65.0 points of tool correctness (P3452).
items.why: Solid. 4 papers, B yes in P2749, P1656 and P3452 and C yes in P1656, P2858 and P3452, over Qwen, Llama, Gemma, Phi and Falcon models. The one family paper that shows a related tool-turn correctness probe failing (P2456, on contaminated histories) states that failure itself.
items.note: All four are 2026 preprints or workshop papers. When P1656 refits with another solver seed, only 12, 36 and 61 percent of its top-100 neurons for over-calling, missing and validity reproduce, so the readout is not unique even where it works. P2456 shows correctness probes fail on contaminated histories (problematic finding). We could not rebuild the P2749 or P2858 datasets (labels unreleased, code link dead).

items.title: Steering non-English reasoning toward English raises accuracy
items.line: Nudging a model thinking in another language toward its English state makes it reason better while it still answers in the asked language.
items.status: 4 papers, 4 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: Tech Support vector applied to Finance, gain against within-domain gain

quote.text: leading to an average improvement of 5.48% on four benchmarks, while improving input-output language consistency by 3.78%

items.technical: Shifting non-dominant-language hidden states toward English by difference-of-means or erasure-based vectors, then restoring language identity, improves multilingual reasoning benchmarks by a few points.
items.why: Solid by the literature rule. 4 papers in the family report it, 1 with held-out accuracy (rubric B yes) and 4 with a measured intervention (rubric C yes), over 6 open model families (Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Phi, Qwen, Vision-language). The one documented weakness, loss of gain across domains in P3074, is qualified by its authors, who recommend calibrating per domain.
items.note: P2417 makes the same claim for Hindi and Spanish but several of its appendix tables call their numbers illustrative placeholders, so it is left out of the support. Gains are modest, about five points on average in P0326. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P3074).

items.title: Grammaticality can be read off and is not just likelihood
items.line: A simple probe tells grammatical from broken sentences and does better than the model's own sentence probabilities.
items.status: 5 papers, 4 with held-out accuracy

quote.text: We find that this simple grammaticality probe generalizes to human-curated grammaticality judgment benchmarks

items.technical: Linear probes and mass-mean directions separate grammatical from ungrammatical sentences on held-out BLiMP, CoLA and SyntaxGym items, beat string log-probability, and peak in early to middle layers.
items.why: Solid by the literature rule. 5 papers in the family report it, 4 with held-out accuracy (rubric B yes) and 0 with a measured intervention (rubric C yes), over 6 open model families (GPT-2, Gemma, Llama, OLMo, Pythia/GPT-NeoX, Qwen). None of them contradict decodability.
items.note: Our own difference of means at Llama-3-8B-Instruct layer 16 reads BLiMP phenomena only at about 0.73 even within a phenomenon, so the strong results may depend on a trained probe, a chosen layer or a larger model, which we have not tested. Our Shakespeare link also suggests the arrow partly tracks how usual a sentence looks.

items.title: The language part of a representation can be cut away
items.line: Removing a small language-specific part leaves meaning that lines up across languages, and removing one language's features hurts mainly that language.
items.status: 4 papers, 4 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: Cross-language answer retrieval, average off-diagonal score after and before removing the language subspace (mBERT, XQuAD-R)

quote.text: Once the subspace is found, we can directly project the original embeddings into the null space to boost language agnosticism without finetuning.

items.technical: Projecting out a low-rank language subspace (SVD of language means, INLP or LEACE) makes multilingual representations more language-agnostic and improves cross-lingual retrieval and alignment, and ablating monolingual SAE features degrades mainly the matching language.
items.why: Solid by the literature rule. 4 papers in the family report it, 1 with held-out accuracy (rubric B yes) and 4 with a measured intervention (rubric C yes), over 4 open model families (BERT-family, Gemma, Llama, Qwen). The limit in P2987, that most translation information is non-linear, is stated by its authors.
items.note: This is the erasure side of the language findings above. P0507 and P2987 are older encoder studies (2022 and 2020), while P1897 and P0209 carry it to Gemma, Llama and Qwen. P0281 adds that romanized text falls outside the native-script language region, so script may escape a subspace fitted on native script. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P2987).

items.title: Agent roles, memories and agent training weaken refusal signals
items.line: Giving a model an agent role, personal memories or agentic training moves its hidden states away from refusal and toward the harmful side.
items.status: 4 papers, 3 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: P0395 attack success after the refusal-direction intervention

quote.text: role assignment suppresses refusal awareness by shifting representations away from safety boundaries

items.technical: Role assignment in deep-research agents shifts representations away from the refusal-probe boundary (P0395, QwQ-32B), agentic RL for search progressively shifts search behaviour toward the harmful end of a difference-of-means direction that causally controls search-query safety (P3335, Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3.2), retrieved personal memories shift harmful queries toward the benign side of a harmful-intent direction (P0334), and agentic fine-tuning leaves web agents refusing 0 percent of harmful tasks with low harm-probe logits, which steering along the probe restores (P0125).
items.why: Solid. 4 papers report it, B yes in P0395 and C yes in P0395, P3335 and P0125, over Qwen, QwQ, Llama and DeepSeek backbones, and we found no paper showing the shift absent. Each route (role, memory, RL, fine-tuning) rests on one paper, so the shared claim is solid while each route is unreplicated.
items.note: All four are 2026 papers. P0334 and P0125 are coded refusal only, so outside the family by concept code. P0334's evidence is a principal-component picture (B partial, C no) and P0125's is low probe logits in fine-tuned agents without a before-and-after comparison, so the representational side is thinner than the behavioural one. P0395 probes only the final layer with no stated reason, and P3335 picks its layer on the held-out evaluation prompts (our layer coding).

items.title: Deleting a topic's features removes it and spares other text
items.line: Switching off the units or features tied to one topic, class or figure of speech removes that ability while other content mostly survives.
items.status: 4 papers, 4 with a measured intervention

quote.text: enabling the unlearning of specific topics while preserving overall model performance on unrelated tasks

items.technical: Deleting topic-enriched codebook features, gated difference-of-means removal of OneSeC concepts, ablating class-specific SAE feature segments and adaptive masking of rhetoric-selective neurons reduce the targeted topic, class or device while keeping unrelated performance within a budget, though plain zero or mean masking can misbehave.
items.why: Solid by the literature rule. 4 papers in the family report it, 0 with held-out accuracy (rubric B yes) and 4 with a measured intervention (rubric C yes), over 6 open model families (BERT-family, Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Pythia/GPT-NeoX, Qwen). The masking failures in P0217 are reported and explained by its authors.
items.note: The estimators differ (codebook features on T5-small in P3145, gated mean-difference vectors in P2116, SAE segments in P0793, neurons in P0217), so the shared lesson is that removal works when the removed part is selected for the concept, not that one method does. The contrary case for linguistic features is P0777, in the finding on readable but unused features. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0217).

items.title: Models default to Western culture, and culture arrows redirect them
items.line: Asked vaguely, models mostly answer as if the user were American or British, and a culture direction can steer answers toward another culture.
items.status: 4 papers, 4 with a measured intervention

numbers.label: share of underspecified-prompt answers defaulting to the US and the UK, Gemma-2-9B
culture MCQ accuracy after ablating the top-10 culture features at layer 23

quote.text: 33.1% of responses align most closely with the U.S. and 26.9% with the U.K., together accounting for roughly 60% of cultural defaults

items.technical: Culture directions from SAE features or contrastive activations show US and UK defaults under underspecified prompts, their ablation degrades culturally conditioned answers, and adding them increases localisation beyond prompting.
items.why: Solid by the literature rule. 4 papers report it, 4 with a measured intervention, over 3 open model families (Gemma, Llama, Qwen), and none finds the default absent.
items.note: Steering works unevenly. P0427 says effectiveness varies substantially across countries, P0570 finds global knowledge categories hard to align, and P0736's universal vector trails culture-specific ones. Our reading of P0736 data is in the gender and culture finding above.

items.title: Activation probes catch deceiving, colluding or hijacked agents
items.line: Probes on an agent's activations flag deception, collusion and compromise better than monitors that read only its actions and outputs.
items.status: 4 papers, 1 with a measured intervention, 3 with held-out accuracy, 1 against

numbers.label: P1920 mean pAUROC gain of white-box over black-box monitors
P1347 F1 vs graph-based baseline, synchronous setting

quote.text: generalize extremely well out-of-distribution, consistently obtaining AUROCs over 95%

items.technical: Logistic-regression probes and centroid detectors on agent hidden states detect deception in Among Us with AUROC above 0.95 out of distribution (P1491), deception across 12 categories with a mean pAUROC gain of 0.097 over black-box monitors (P1920), collusion in multi-agent games (P2966), and compromised agents at F1 0.94 against 0.72 for graph-based baselines (P1347).
items.why: Solid. 4 papers, B yes in P1491, P1920 and P1347, over Phi-4, Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen3 and other backbones. Both limits (no transfer to TruthfulQA, failure under domain shift) are qualified by the papers that find them.
items.note: P1491 and P1347 are in both lists because they report the effect and its limit, and the limits are collected in a separate problematic finding. P3563 (workshop 2026, coded refusal only) shows prompt-injection probes on InjecAgent and AgentDojo tracking cue words, which bears on the compromised-agent part through P1347's InjecAgent data though not on the deception and collusion probes. Three of the four are 2026 papers and P1920 and P2966 are unreviewed preprints. P1920 trains on synthetic trajectories and our record found no resampling check of its probe. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P1347, P1491).

items.title: Task encoding emerges in training and tracks ICL skill
items.line: Clear internal task codes appear partway through training, and how clearly a model codes a task predicts how well it learns it from examples.
items.status: 4 papers, 3 with a measured intervention

quote.text: we demonstrate that the quality of task encoding inferred from representations predicts ICL performance

items.technical: Task vectors and linear steerability emerge at intermediate stages of pretraining, task-encoding quality read from representations predicts ICL performance across Gemma, Llama and OLMo, and function-vector similarity predicts which tasks follow similar training trajectories, though task vectors can be weakly or non-locally encoded in small from-scratch models.
items.why: Four family papers with measured interventions (C yes for P1185, P0384 and P0848) across Gemma, Llama, OLMo, Pythia and GPT-2, and no contrary paper.
items.note: P0384 qualifies that task vectors emerge only under some conditions. P0438's prediction rests on function vectors it checked for split-half stability. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0384).

items.title: Small trained vectors recover most of what RL training adds
items.line: A few added vectors trained with the RL objective get back most of the math accuracy that full RL fine-tuning brings.
items.status: 3 papers, 3 with a measured intervention

numbers.label: share of RL gain recovered by steering RL-enhanced SAE features
share of full-tuning gain recovered by steering vectors in LLaMa3.1-8B

quote.text: Table 1 shows that steering vectors match the accuracy of fully tuned models across families and scales. The only exception is LLaMa3.1-8B, where steering recovers about 70% of the full-tuning gain.

items.technical: Additive steering vectors trained with an RL objective, or SAE features amplified by RL and steered into the base model, match or recover most of the math-accuracy gain of full RL fine-tuning in Qwen and Llama models, supporting the view that RL mainly draws out abilities already present.
items.why: Three papers with measured interventions (C yes) across Qwen and Llama, and none contrary.
items.note: The vectors in P0607 and P3288 are trained, not read from data, so this says RL gains fit in a few vectors rather than that a concept direction was found. P0607 and P3288 come from the same T-Tech group (Sinii and coauthors), so only two independent groups back this. P2901 is a September 2026 preprint on Qwen only.

items.title: Warmth and competence stereotypes can be read from inside
items.line: The two classic stereotype scales, how warm and how competent a group seems, can be read from the model's insides.
items.status: 3 papers, 1 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: held-out impression probe accuracy, warmth and competence

quote.text: Probe accuracies (80-90% for warmth, 75%-85% for competence; included in Appendix H) exceed self-consistency scores in the third-person setting (Table 1).

items.technical: Probes or semantic axes on heads, MLP or residual activations predict warmth and competence ratings of social groups or prompt authors. Steering along them is not solid, since P0108's steering reverses for one subgroup without the claim being qualified.
items.why: Solid by the literature rule. 3 papers report it, 1 with held-out accuracy and 1 with a measured intervention, over 5 open model families (DeepSeek, Llama, Mistral, OLMo, Qwen).
items.note: Reading is solid, steering is not, since P0108's steering reverses for one subgroup (above). P2625 finds model stereotype content diverges from human ratings, so what the axes hold is the model's own view. P0108 does not state whether its head correlations are held out (B partial).

items.title: Grammatical features share arrows across languages
items.line: Number and gender are coded by directions many languages share, and removing the shared ones breaks the readout in every language.
items.status: 3 papers, 3 with a measured intervention, 1 against

numbers.label: Our reading of held-out languages by one pooled difference of means, Morphosyntax (P1378 data), median
Same, weakest language (Indonesian)

quote.text: adding PC1English successfully flips the Spanish verb number prediction to plural

items.technical: A subject-number direction found in English flips Spanish verb agreement, multilingual SAE features for case, gender, number and tense are causally needed across 23 languages, and language-neutral axes carry part of speech in XLM-R.
items.why: Solid by the literature rule, narrowly. 3 papers in the family report it, 0 with held-out accuracy (rubric B yes) and 3 with a measured intervention (rubric C yes), over 3 open model families (BERT-family, Gemma, Llama). The one limit, P0365 finding only limited cross-lingual alignment of phenomena, is qualified by its authors.
items.note: Our single difference of means at layer 16 reads the P1378 items only moderately, and about as poorly within each language (within mean 0.742, loso_detection.json), so the modest numbers reflect our estimator and reading rather than a transfer failure. P0280 finds inflection decodable in 25 models and 6 languages but fits a probe per language, so it shows decodability, not a shared arrow. P0365 compares per-item minimal-pair differences rather than fitted directions.

themes.title: Shaky findings and open problems
themes.blurb: Thin, in-sample or contested findings, and problems the papers themselves call unsolved.

items.title: Directions often break when the data change
items.line: An arrow learned on one set of examples often weakens when wording, topic, format or conversation length changes, and only partial fixes exist.
items.status: named by 124 papers

numbers.label: papers naming the problem
negative results, grouping pass count
papers that read a direction on a group held out of the fit
weighted share of all 881 running that held-out group check
member papers kept after the verifier read their extracted statements

quote.text: probes fail to generalize under important production distribution shifts

items.technical: 131 papers state that probes and steering vectors fit on one prompt distribution degrade under dataset, domain, template, negation, synthetic-to-natural, single-to-multi-turn or short-to-long generation shift, and no extracted statement claims a remedy.
items.why: Shaky because the papers themselves name it as unsolved. 131 papers state it, with by_type counts of 40 open problem, 67 limitation and 35 negative result from the grouping pass, and the pass rated it hard. Fixes are partial and contested, not absent.
items.note: Progress, partial. P0720 reports that moving the probe to another layer or making it nonlinear does not repair the out-of-distribution drop. Three papers claim partial remedies, a two-dimensional truth subspace that explains the negation failure (P1482), training on more diverse datasets (P0539) and style-augmented probes that recover under stylistic shift (P3104), and P2235 lists the P1482 repair of negation as still untested on its own data. P0192 finds prompts make the structure more consistent across domains, and P1436 finds steering vectors often generalise well. Our work bears on it. Our held-out group reading scores a group the direction was not fitted on, one kind of shift the papers worry about, and the pooled direction reads such a group at a median AUROC of 0.959 over 880 groups while 81 groups in 25 datasets fall below 0.7 (runs/soundness/corpus72.json loso.canonical72). The member list comes from one model grouping pass with no second coder. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0192, P1436, P1482, P3104).

items.title: The arrow may follow a stand-in, not the concept
items.line: An arrow built from two contrasting example sets absorbs every difference between them, so a working detector may be reading wording or style instead.
items.status: named by 126 papers

numbers.label: papers naming the problem
negative results, grouping pass count
member papers kept after the verifier read their extracted statements

quote.text: probes mainly memorise lexical patterns from the training distribution rather than capturing semantic intent

items.technical: 130 papers state that difference-of-means and probe directions absorb confounds of the contrast set, such as lexical cues, style, topic, length, base rates and the labeller's proxy, so decoding or steering success does not fix what the direction encodes.
items.why: Shaky because the papers themselves name it as unsolved. 130 papers state it, with by_type counts of 34 open problem, 85 limitation and 22 negative result from the grouping pass, and the pass rated it hard. The pass records no claimed fix.
items.note: Progress. Only partial safeguards are named, reporting selectivity against control tasks (P0280, and the control-task paper P3701, a recall addition outside the extraction) and adding lexical controls to benchmarks (P3563). P0720 finds nonlinear probes keep the same reliance on surface patterns. Our work bears on it. A rule named before capture, that behaviours an aligned assistant would disavow are read backwards, put 5 of 6 new disavowed behaviours below chance at Llama-3-8B-Instruct and held at the two newer Llama readings but missed its bar at both Qwen readings, and three registered searches for misread groups without knowing the shortcut failed (SURVEY/data/factsheet.json final ids persona-named-in-advance and proxy-search-fails). No routine check in the papers settles this problem, so the survey maps it to no rubric column.

items.title: Readable is not the same as used
items.line: Reading a concept from the activations does not show the model uses it, and a working push need not be how the model works.

quote.text: linear separability does not itself imply linear controllability

items.technical: 106 papers state that probe decodability, causal use and steerability come apart, with decodable directions lacking causal effect, probe accuracy failing to predict steering, steering effects invisible to decoders (P3539) and sufficiency shown without necessity (P3548).
items.why: Shaky because the papers themselves name it as unsolved. 106 papers state it, with by_type counts of 22 open problem, 47 limitation and 45 negative result from the grouping pass, and the pass rated it hard. It has the most negative results of any cluster.
items.note: Progress. No statement claims to close the gap. P1805 says steering overstates control. This is the one problem that is routinely tested, since most papers measure an intervention, a separate count finding in this file. Our work bears on it directly. Our registered steering test of four concept links came out INCONCLUSIVE because well-read arrows mostly did not move the model's own answers, a separate finding in this file.

items.title: One straight line may not capture the concept
items.line: Many concepts look like several dials, a curved surface or a region, so a single arrow captures only part of them.
items.status: named by 128 papers

numbers.label: papers naming the problem
negative results, grouping pass count
member papers kept after the verifier read their extracted statements

quote.text: We establish that refusal behaviors can be better understood via high-dimensional polyhedral cones in activation space rather than a single linear direction, highlighting their complex spatial structures.

items.technical: 130 papers state that the single-direction linear representation assumption fails for multi-dimensional, multi-valued, curved or nonlinearly encoded concepts, and one gives a formal rank-one limit for task vectors on general bijections (P1113).
items.why: Shaky because the papers themselves name it as unsolved. 130 papers state it, with by_type counts of 42 open problem, 83 limitation and 16 negative result from the grouping pass, and the pass rated it hard. Progress is partial, and the rank-one result is an impossibility claim.
items.note: Progress, partial. Papers propose refusal cones (P1215), several directions or a manifold (P0110), geometry-aware steering tried only on simple concepts (P0409) and nonlinear transport (P1639). Against the need for more, P1475 finds refusal mediated by a single direction across open chat models, which P1215 and P0110 contest for the same concept, and P1533 finds higher-rank interventions underperform rank-1 steering on larger models. Our work bears on it, exploratory. A label-free five-dimensional subspace lifts only 2 of 19 backwards groups to 0.7 or better, though the same span holds a reader for 14 of 19 when the held-out labels are used (SURVEY/data/factsheet.json final id fit-time-remedies, status exploratory-unregistered). Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P1533).

items.title: No answer key to grade directions against
items.line: For most concepts nobody knows what the model truly represents, so papers grade arrows with AI judges, proxy scores or best-case numbers that can mislead.
items.status: named by 111 papers

numbers.label: papers naming the problem
negative results, grouping pass count

quote.text: A big problem in interpretability research is the lack of "ground truth".

items.technical: 118 papers state that evaluation lacks ground-truth concepts and labels, that LLM judges are prompt-sensitive and disagree with humans (P1253, P3548), that best-of-grid numbers overstate effects, and that steering often loses to prompting or fine-tuning when compared (P0398, P1178, P3186).
items.why: Shaky because the papers themselves name it as unsolved. 118 papers state it, with by_type counts of 27 open problem, 73 limitation and 26 negative result from the grouping pass, and the pass rated it hard. The pass records no claimed fix.
items.note: Progress. P0682 injects a known algorithm into a pretrained model to create a ground truth, but reports that the model does not represent the injected variables on inputs far outside training, and P1176 points to toy models whose true features are known. Neither gives ground truth for natural concepts. Our work bears on it. Every label-free route we tried to find misread groups fell short, which is a separate finding in this file.

items.title: Choosing layer, strength and token is trial and error
items.line: Results depend heavily on where you read or push, how hard, and at which word, and these are still picked by search for every model.
items.status: named by 107 papers

numbers.label: papers naming the problem
negative results, grouping pass count

quote.text: we lack a principled way to select the best layer

items.technical: 107 papers state that layer, coefficient, token position, pooling and subspace size are set by per-model grid search, that the same coefficient acts differently on each token (P3323), and that effects are non-monotonic in strength and can reverse (P1727).
items.why: Shaky because the papers themselves name it as unsolved. 107 papers state it, with by_type counts of 28 open problem, 70 limitation and 15 negative result from the grouping pass, and the pass rated it open but tractable. It is the only cluster the pass rates tractable, an engineering search.
items.note: Progress, partial. Adaptive steering intensity exists but is set by heuristic (P1504), and no statement claims a principled rule. A remedy is known, choosing the setting on held-out data, since P2943 (a member of other clusters) notes best-of-grid numbers overstate a preselected setting, and some papers use it (layer-choice finding in this file). Our work bears on it. How papers choose the layer is a separate registered count, and our depth sweep shows the layer can decide whether groups share one direction, both separate findings in this file.

items.title: The same concept can yield many different arrows
items.line: Rebuilding a concept's arrow from another sample, seed, dataset or method can give a different arrow that works just as well.

quote.text: infinitely many geometrically distinct directions produce equivalent behavioral effects due to the large null space of the activation-to-output Jacobian.

items.technical: 100 papers state that concept directions are non-identifiable, with many distinct or orthogonal directions giving equal probe accuracy or steering effect (P3128, P3482), SAE features differing across seeds (P1097), few-pair estimates being imprecise (P2181) and directions rotating under fine-tuning.
items.why: Shaky because the papers themselves name it as unsolved. 100 papers state it, with by_type counts of 25 open problem, 62 limitation and 22 negative result from the grouping pass, and the pass rated it hard. There are formal non-identifiability results and no tested fix.
items.note: Progress. Structural constraints such as sparsity or invariance are proposed to make directions identifiable but not tested (P2445, P3482). Of the 40 papers that report refit stability (rubric A yes), 9 are members of this cluster (P0510, P1097, P1245, P1254, P1824, P2181, P2526, P3035, P3324). P2445 and P3482 are preprint and workshop versions of one paper (SURVEY/paper/sections/openproblems.numbers.json notes), so they are one voice counted twice. Our work bears on it. A direction can be highly repeatable and still average groups that disagree, a separate finding in this file.

items.line: Steering along one arrow also shifts fluency, other traits, general skills or safety, sometimes in places nobody checked.

numbers.label: papers naming the problem

quote.text: Even when strong global constraints such as symmetric orthonormalisation are applied, steering one trait consistently induces measurable changes in other unintended traits, indicating persistent cross-trait dependencies.

items.technical: 97 papers state that steering causes off-target concept shifts, loss of coherence and capability, over-refusal and weaker refusal, even with random (P3568) or benign (P0690) vectors, and that orthogonalizing directions does not stop behavioural spillover (P0711).
items.why: Shaky because the papers themselves name it as unsolved. 97 papers state it, with by_type counts of 28 open problem, 43 limitation and 43 negative result from the grouping pass, and the pass rated it hard. The pass records no claimed fix.
items.note: Progress, partial. P0422 reports a post-hoc correction that substantially reduces the safety cost of steering while keeping the steering effect, so the safety part of the problem has a claimed partial fix. Orthogonalization is tried and still spills over (P0711), and P2373 asks whether the trade-off between control and capability is fundamental. Something directions do well sits inside the problem, since P2026 finds the target scores shift consistently across models even while other dimensions move. P3528 and P3599 are two versions of one paper by the same authors with identical extracted statements, so they are one voice counted twice. Our work does not measure side effects (SURVEY/paper/sections/openproblems.tex, What our re-measurement adds). Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0422).

items.title: Arrows often fail to carry across models
items.line: A recipe that works on one model often weakens or flips on another model, size, language or input type, and nobody can say why.
items.status: named by 78 papers

numbers.label: papers naming the problem
negative results, grouping pass count

quote.text: The emotion-based behavior shift is not predictably transferable across models

items.technical: 78 papers state that directions, best layers and signal polarity are specific to model, family, scale and modality, that cross-model steering transfer works only in specific cases, that cross-lingual transfer is uneven and that effects can reverse with scale.
items.why: Shaky because the papers themselves name it as unsolved. 78 papers state it, with by_type counts of 25 open problem, 32 limitation and 31 negative result from the grouping pass, and the pass rated it medium. The pass notes that testing needs only more open models, and the open part is explaining why models differ.
items.note: Progress, partial. Mappings across architectures carry behavioural influence but lose concept specificity (P1696), and feed-forward coordinate transport across models is less stable over long horizons (P2673). P0032 finds probing and steering tools largely carry over to RNNs, and P2026 finds target scores shift consistently across models, which limit the claim, and P1571 finds a refusal direction taken from English bypasses refusal in other languages with near-perfect effect. Our work bears on it, exploratory. Per-group AUROC over 682 groups in 56 datasets correlates across five model readings at Spearman 0.724 to 0.820 within a family and 0.538 to 0.679 across families, yet only 4 of the 49 groups read below chance at some reading do so at all five (SURVEY/data/factsheet.json final id cross-model-groups, status exploratory-unregistered). Part of the Llama and Qwen gap on truth data is where the model is read (depth-sweep finding in this file). Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0032, P1571).

quote.text: Our results suggest that vector steering is unreliable when the target behavior is not represented by a coherent direction.

items.technical: 73 papers state that concept directions rotate with context, persona, prompt format or subtype, that a pooled difference of means averages heterogeneous clusters, and that aggregate success hides item and slice reversals (P1436, P3308, P2794, P3086).

items.note: This is the problem our survey and paper are about. Progress, partial. Conditional, gated or adaptive steering is proposed (P2116, P1504, P0237), but P0248 reports that earlier conditional gates fail to generalise over varied inputs and P1504 sets its adaptivity by heuristic. Only 6 of 881 papers fit a direction per group, compare them and show they are stable (P1348, P1844, P2181, P2800, P3308, P3324), and only P3308 of them is a member of this cluster. Our work bears on it most directly. Over 880 held-out groups the pooled direction reads at a median AUROC of 0.959, and 17 of the 18 backwards groups have a negative cosine with the pooled direction while all 19 negative-cosine groups read below 0.7 (runs/soundness/corpus72.json loso.canonical72.principle). P1646 adds that the model can group a sentence differently from its dataset label, so a group check needs the right groups. The 880 groups include four of our rebuilds later found faulty (P1074, P2800, P0973 and P1216), and the self-recognition case (P0973) falls. The authors chose to drop them from the survey website only (RUNLOG.md 2026-09-26 10.34), which gives 850 groups, 17 below chance and 79 below 0.7 (SURVEY/web/data.json headline), while the paper and corpus72.json keep 880, 18 and 81 and recounting the paper is still open.

items.technical: The direction-agreement check (settled E yes, per-group directions compared with resampling stability beside them) is run by 6 of 881 papers (1.3 percent weighted), per-group directions are compared at all by 11.2 percent (15.1 percent after correcting for partial marks one reading misses), and their results conflict. Refusal categories sit at cosines of 0.4 to 0.6 against 0.96 resampling stability (P2800), prompt-type vectors at 0.07 to 0.86 (P3308), syntax has no common direction across languages while pragmatics agrees at 0.92 (P1844), refusal category subspaces overlap heterogeneously once shared decision variance is removed (P3324), moral-foundation directions from two datasets align only weakly at absolute cosines of 0.07 to 0.21 (P2181), and only code-security vectors across programming languages clearly agree, at cosines of 0.58 to 0.95 (P1348).
items.why: Reported by only six papers, five of them from 2026 and one from a main venue (IEEE EuroS&P, off the venue list), with results that conflict by concept, so what the check finds is unsettled.
items.note: P1348 stability evidence is the weakest the rubric accepts, a running vector compared with the final one, which agree by construction (evidence.tex lines 214-217). Only 59 of the 358 reading-check papers compare per-group directions (evidence.tex line 165). Design interval for settled E yes 0.0062 to 0.02666 (precision.json intervals.E_settled_yes.wilson95_design). P1844 finds pragmatics agreeing at 0.92 and syntax at 0.00 in one paper, so agreement varies within a concept family too. P1348 Table 2 cosines between Python, C++ and Java code-security vectors run from 0.58 to 0.95 (full text lines 707-723). P2181 reads its 0.07 to 0.21 as positive alignment and attributes the small size to 30 external vignettes (full text lines 2073-2074), while its own bootstrap stability bar is a cosine above 0.8 (lines 268-269). Merged from 2 verified findings across cross-cutting (prac06, open17). The family readers placed these under shaky, solid; the editor placed the merged item under shaky. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P1348).

items.title: Whether plain prompting beats steering is contested
items.line: Benchmarks often find simply asking the model beats steering, while many papers proposing a steering method report beating a prompting baseline.
items.status: 4 papers for, 6 against

quote.text: For steering, we find that prompting outperforms all existing methods, followed by finetuning.

items.technical: On AxBench prompting outperforms every steering method on Gemma-2 (P1178), on human-similarity judgments SAEs, task vectors and DiffMean all do worse than prompting (P0398), prompting beats feature steering at both model scales in a capability study (P2373) and persona prompting beats more complex interventions for cross-lingual answers (P3075), while on cross-lingual steering DiffMean beats every method including prompting across most languages (P0696), and many method papers report their steering beating a prompting baseline, among them bias mitigation (P0792), reasoning control (P0231, P1290) and concept steering (P3473).
items.why: Contested between many papers on both sides, on different tasks and models, so shaky.
items.note: We did not count how many steering papers compare against a prompting baseline, so the lists are examples found by a corpus search in this run. The papers favouring prompting are mostly evaluations and benchmarks, and most papers favouring steering propose the steering method they test, so which side a paper lands on may track its purpose. P1315 states that activation steering methods still struggle to outperform prompting (full text lines 36-37) and then reports its own prompt-imitating method beating prompt steering.

items.title: The token read is often unstated, and its effect disputed
items.line: One paper in six never says which word position it reads, and papers disagree on how much that choice changes the result.
items.status: 144 papers leave the token unstated

numbers.label: token position unstated (count, weighted share)

quote.text: Holding the downstream intervention fixed, we show across three instruction-tuned models and four steering task families that changing only the source activations substantially changes steering success

items.technical: 144 papers (17.1 percent weighted) do not state which token position they read, the final token is the most common read (35.4 percent) and 21.6 percent compare more than one position, while papers report both strong sensitivity to the position or source of the activations (P2943, P1315) or call the position crucial (P3588), and near-invariance within a layer block (P3500), and 107 papers name layer, strength and token choice as unsolved.
items.why: Contested between papers and named as unsolved by 107 papers (28 as an open problem, 70 as a limitation, 15 with a negative result, open_problems.json synth.problems[14].by_type), so shaky.
items.note: The registered prediction that at most 20 percent compare more than one token missed narrowly (lt_coding.json summary.P4_T2_yes_at_most_20pct false). T2 kappa 0.694 is the lowest of the layer and token codes. P2943 (2026) adds that steering signals work best from execution-boundary states where the model is about to act, a claim not yet replicated in the corpus.

items.title: Evidence habits have not clearly changed since 2024
items.line: From 2024 to 2026 stability checks crept up and held-out accuracy slipped a little, but neither change is beyond chance.
items.status: corpus count by year, not settled

items.title: Steering for better reasoning accuracy gives small, uneven gains
items.line: Pushing a model along a reasoning direction usually raises accuracy by a few points, and on some models or tests not at all.
items.status: 11 papers, 11 with a measured intervention, 7 against

numbers.label: average gain from extracted CoT vectors on two models
largest gain from conditional steering on syllogisms

quote.text: Control vector-based methods achieve only marginal improvements in almost all tasks

items.technical: Accuracy gains from reasoning steering vectors (chain-of-thought, correctness, logic and domain vectors) are often a few points and vary by model and benchmark (marginal for linear control vectors in base models, none on MATH levels 3 and 4, negative in some Llama settings), while other papers report gains of 10 points or more.
items.why: Contested between papers. Eleven family papers report marginal or uneven gains and seven report large ones, on different models, tasks and baselines.
items.note: Gains are hard to compare because baselines, decoding and layer choice differ, and many layers were chosen on the test data. Length control (the reflection finding) is much more consistent than accuracy gains.

items.title: One fixed vector underfits varied harmful inputs
items.line: Harmful requests fall into kinds, and methods that adjust the push to each input beat one fixed arrow on the tests reported.
items.status: 7 papers, 7 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy, 1 against

quote.text: renders global steering directions brittle

items.technical: Harmful-instruction activations form semantic clusters (P1240), the safe behavior differs by request type such as abstaining against referring to an expert (P1548), and input-adaptive steering (cluster optimal transport, learned per-input vectors, invertible latent maps, query-adaptive bridges, dynamic element masks, token-aware editing) outperforms one global difference-of-means vector on the benchmarks each paper reports.
items.why: Shaky. Seven papers report gains, but each measures its own method against baselines it ran with no independent comparison, and P2800's one-knob result suggests one direction already captures most control over whether to refuse.
items.note: P1240 reports ASR gains of up to 7 percent over ActAdd, so the margins are modest.

items.title: Whether sparse features beat simple directions is contested
items.line: Some papers find sparse autoencoder features trail plain directions for detection and steering, others find them competitive.
items.status: 9 papers, 8 with a measured intervention, 5 with held-out accuracy, 10 against
