quote.text: For steering, we find that prompting outperforms all existing methods, followed by finetuning. For concept detection, representation-based methods such as difference-in-means, perform the best. On both evaluations, SAEs are not competitive.

items.technical: AxBench finds SAEs not competitive for steering or detection on Gemma-2 (P1178), SAE-based probes fail to beat baselines consistently across four hard regimes (P1176), and feature absorption makes SAE latents unreliable classifiers (P1489), while SAE directions beat DiffMean for concept insertion and suppression in a vision-language model (P1583) and a bidirectional AbsTopK SAE matches or surpasses DiffMean (P1020).
items.why: Contested between papers, with newer SAE variants and one vision-language study reporting the opposite, so shaky.
items.note: SAE papers report results by group least often of any estimator, with a Kish interval of 0.3445 to 0.5536 that overlaps others (precision.json kish_rows.estimator.SAE-dictionary.D). Our own SAE per-group check was withdrawn over a tie-ranking bug (factsheet.json estimators-and-sae caveats). Merged from 3 verified findings across cross-cutting, other, style-language (prac12, othe19, styl19).

items.title: Moving a direction to another model needs care
items.line: Whether a direction carries to a different model or version is contested, and it often needs mapping or refitting.
items.status: 9 papers, 8 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy, 5 against

numbers.label: [emotion-bias] sentiment steering effect kept after transport with sign-aware gauge versus permutation only

quote.text: aligned using simple linear transformations, enabling efficient cross-model transfer and behavioral control via SVs.

items.technical: Linear maps align concept steering vectors across LLMs and allow weak-to-strong control, and optimised vectors transfer across models and LoRAs, but ridge-mapped misalignment directions suppress behaviour about as much as random or orthogonal controls, and permutation-only coordinate transport reverses refusal steering in RMSNorm models.
items.why: Shaky, contested. P0168 and P1471 report working transfer, while P1696 finds it non-specific and P2673 shows it breaks without the right coordinate alignment.
items.note: The positive reports mostly move between closely related Llama and Qwen models or between LoRAs of one base. None of the four checks transfer with a held-out accuracy of the mapped direction. Merged from 3 verified findings across persona-sycophancy, emotion-bias, refusal-safety (pers29, emot08, rste06). Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0375, P2673).

items.title: Whether bigger models hold more general truth is unsettled
items.line: Several papers find larger models carry a cleaner truth arrow, but deception and hallucination readers grow more narrow as models grow.
items.status: 5 papers, 4 with a measured intervention, 5 with held-out accuracy, 2 against

numbers.label: RepE-trained deception probe read on MASK at 1B, 4B, 12B, 27B
Topics where negation generalises, Llama-2-7B against Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct

quote.text: For Llama-2-7B(-Chat), the probes fail to generalize on all six topics.

items.technical: Truth-direction consistency and probe generalisation improve with model capability in several papers (all six negation topics fail for Llama-2-7B and pass for Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct in P0673), while deception types become more domain-specific with scale (P3104) and cross-benchmark hallucination transfer diminishes at larger scale (P1707).
items.why: 5 supporting papers, 5 with B yes and 4 with C yes, across 7 coded model families. Shaky because contested, 5 papers report gains with scale for truth, 2 report narrowing with scale for deception and hallucination transfer.
items.note: The two sides measure different things (statement truth against deception or hallucination detectors), so they may not conflict. P1103 finds its probe works for larger models and fails for smaller ones (line 598).

items.title: Probes beat stated confidence only in some settings
items.line: Reading the insides beats asking the model how sure it is when the model is confidently wrong, but the edge shrinks on ordinary questions.
items.status: 8 papers, 2 with a measured intervention, 7 with held-out accuracy, 4 against

numbers.label: MMLU AUROC, max softmax against raw-neuron probe, Llama-3.1-8B
MMLU AUROC, max softmax against raw-neuron probe, Qwen3-8B
P(True) on SciQ, CSQA and FEVER, Qwen2-7B

quote.text: probes far outperform P(True) and semantic entropy on adversarial misconceptions but tie on standard QA

items.technical: Hidden-state probes outperform verbal confidence, P(True), entropy or max softmax on adversarial misconception data and some RAG settings, but tie or barely beat output-based signals on standard QA and multiple-choice tasks.
items.why: Shaky because it is contested, 8 records support it and 5 limit or contradict it, with P0223 on both sides and P3205 and P3359 two versions of one paper.
items.note: P3560 supports and limits the claim in the same paper. P0223 finds probes conservative and weaker than verbalised confidence on easier datasets. P2563's correctness probe only matches the behavioural baseline. The P3359 quote states the paper's starting point, and its own table is mixed, a raw-neuron probe barely beats max softmax on Llama-3.1-8B but beats it clearly on Qwen3-8B (the numbers above), so it limits the claim rather than refutes it. P3205 and P3359 are two versions of one paper, the 2025 arXiv version and the ICLR 2026 workshop version (SURVEY/data/lt_coding.json row P3359 note reads 'Same design as P3205 (later version)'), so they count as one work here. P0223 reports probes calibrating LLM judges substantially better than verbalized and multi-generation baselines (P0223.txt line 88) but underperforming on easier datasets (line 22), so it sits on both sides. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0223).

items.title: One truth direction or many is still contested
items.line: Some papers find one general truth arrow, others find several, a flat plane, or separate arrows for true and false.
items.status: 6 papers, 4 with a measured intervention, 6 with held-out accuracy, 4 against

numbers.label: Mahalanobis cosine between probes predicting cross-domain transfer

quote.text: common probing methods fail to provide a reliable and transferable veracity direction and, in some settings, perform worse than zero-shot prompting; (2) truth and falsehood are not encoded symmetrically; and (3) LLMs encode a third type of signal that is distinct from both true and false.

items.technical: Whether truth has a single universal linear direction is contested, with evidence for a universal two-dimensional subspace (P1482), a spectrum from domain-general to domain-specific directions whose Mahalanobis cosine predicts transfer at R2 0.98 (P2794), asymmetric true and false encodings plus a third neither signal (P3306), skill-specific encodings (P0979) and dataset-specific subspaces (P1235).
items.why: 6 supporting papers, 6 with B yes and 4 with C yes, across 5 coded model families. Shaky because contested, 6 papers argue for several or dataset-specific directions and 4 for a general one.
items.note: The positions partly reconcile, since P1482 and P2794 both find a general direction once training covers the variants. P0979 scores transfer as max(AUC, 1 minus AUC), which by construction hides a backwards read (g_coding note).

items.title: Single papers steer VLM sycophancy, emotion, grounding and referring
items.line: Directions for sycophancy, emotion, GUI grounding, region referring and answer type each change VLM outputs, but each behaviour rests on one paper.
items.status: 6 papers, 6 with a measured intervention

quote.text: steering model behavior away from sycophancy via targeted, inference-time intervention on its internal neural representations

items.technical: Difference-of-means or low-rank subspace directions reduce sycophancy in Video-LLMs across all seven prompt types from a separate calibration set (P0249), inject emotion at middle layers (P1275), carry the causal effect of visual markers on GUI grounding (P0495), improve multi-region referring over tailored models (P1306), shift answer types in fine-tuned MLLMs (P0877), and head selection by a concept dictionary suppresses or enhances concepts in VLM classification and captioning (P1532).
items.why: Shaky. Each behaviour is reported by one paper, none with held-out accuracy (B yes in none of the 6), 4 of 6 choose the layer on evaluation data, and P1306 leaves its own flat OCR and REC subsets unqualified. The broader point that contrastive directions move VLM behaviour is carried by the solid findings above.
items.note: P0495, P0877, P1275 and P1306 choose layers on evaluation data (our layer coding). P0495's direction is a marker-induced subspace applied through neurons chosen per input, and P1532 edits heads rather than adding a vector, so two of the six are not single fixed directions. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P1306).

items.title: Honesty steering helps on average but unevenly
items.line: Pushing an honesty arrow makes models more honest on average, but gains vary by scenario and fail to unlock hidden knowledge.
items.status: 6 papers, 6 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy, 3 against

Best steering score at eliciting hidden capability

quote.text: All methods improve honesty (∼62–77) while preserving coherence (∼87–89), peaking around layer 26.

items.technical: Honesty or deception directions (probe normals, RepE vectors, SAE or transcoder features) shift honesty scores or deceptive outputs when added or subtracted, but effects vary across scenario categories and models, steering fails at eliciting password-locked capabilities (2 percent at best) and trails sampling, few-shot prompting and fine-tuning for eliciting censored knowledge.

items.note: P0388 is on both sides, its Qwen results put some MASK categories below baseline while provided facts gain about 40 points (g_coding). P3364 names sampling without a chat template, few-shot prompting and honesty fine-tuning as the most reliable elicitation methods (lines 36-38). Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0388).

items.title: Middle layers and the last template token work best
items.line: Refusal arrows are usually taken and pushed mid-model at the last token before the answer, though often tuned on test data.
items.status: 6 papers, 6 with a measured intervention, 2 against

quote.text: abstract behaviors (jailbreak, conciseness) favoring middle layers and language favoring earlier layers

items.technical: Abstract behaviors such as jailbreak compliance steer best at middle layers and language at earlier layers (P1861), the strongest steering signals come from execution-boundary states just before the behavior (P2943), middle-layer detoxification beats the last layer (P0655), and masked diffusion models also yield effective directions at pre-instruction tokens (P3330), but refusal expression can be gated at late layers (P3514) and one gradient toxicity subspace works best at the final layer (P1986).
items.why: Shaky. Several papers agree on middle layers, but P1861, P2943 and P0393 chose the layer on the evaluation data (lt_coding L1 swept-test), and P3514 and P1986 point to late layers.
items.note: P2943's execution-boundary result matches our before-the-reply work in spirit, but it was not tested on our data.

items.title: Whether one task vector fits every prompt form is contested
items.line: Some papers find one task vector works across images, languages and wordings, while others find each way of asking builds its own vector.
items.status: 5 papers, 5 with a measured intervention, 1 against

numbers.label: GPT-J present-past function vector accuracy on the template When I think of x, I usually
numbers.value: 16.1% against 49.3% to 67.2% on the other four natural templates

quote.text: We find that VLMs align conceptually equivalent inputs into a shared task vector, which is invariant to modality (text, image) and format (examples, instruction)

items.technical: Cross-modal transfer in vision-language models (P1224), cross-language transfer of translation function vectors (P2045) and natural-text portability (P0912) point to a shared task representation, while demonstration and instruction function vectors rely on different heads (P1512) and function vectors often degrade when extracted in one format and used in another (P1036).
items.why: Contested between papers. Five papers report sharing across form and three report form-dependent vectors or a template where the vector largely fails.
items.note: P1036 is on both sides because its concept vectors hold across formats while its function vectors do not. P0912 is on both sides because it claims portability for all six tasks while one template works far less well. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0912, P1036).

items.title: Whether misalignment shares one direction is contested
items.line: Different bad fine-tunes may land on a similar misalignment direction, but papers disagree and transfer is uneven.
items.status: 6 papers, 5 with a measured intervention, 2 against

numbers.label: [persona-sycophancy] misalignment rate of an OLMo medical-advice model, no ablation, own-direction ablation, insecure-code donor ablation
[refusal-safety] agreement of group directions, Misalignment questions

quote.text: different EM finetunes converge to the same linear representation of general misalignment, which can be used to mediate misaligned behaviour.

items.technical: One line reports that different emergent-misalignment fine-tunes converge to one linear misalignment representation that mediates behaviour, while another finds no general direction transfers (a donor direction from an insecure-code model raises misalignment in a medical-advice model from 4.48 to 15.28 percent) and cross-architecture maps suppress behaviour no more specifically than random directions.
items.why: Shaky, contested between papers. P1052 builds on the convergence result and P1086, P1915 and P2841 find shared persona features or one drift axis across domains, while P2018 and P1696 report the cross-model or cross-fine-tune transfer failing or non-specific. All 6 are from 2026.
items.note: P1052 states convergence as a result it builds on (lines 18-20) rather than a new test in that paper. P1696 compares different architectures, P2018 different fine-tuning datasets on the same base, so they test different kinds of sharing. Merged from 2 verified findings across persona-sycophancy, refusal-safety (pers17, rste15). Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P1052).

items.title: Models may know the user is wrong yet agree anyway
items.line: Some papers find a sycophantic model still registers inside that the user is wrong, while one finds its inner belief itself wears down.
items.status: 3 papers, 3 with a measured intervention, 3 with held-out accuracy, 1 against

numbers.label: sycophancy with the shared heads silenced, Gemma-2-2B (factual accuracy 69 to 70 percent)

quote.text: the same small set of attention heads carries a “this statement is wrong” signal whether the model is evaluating an isolated claim or being pressured to agree with a user.

items.technical: Attention heads carrying a statement-is-wrong signal are shared by sycophancy and lying, and silencing them raises sycophancy from 28 to 81 percent with factual accuracy nearly fixed, and task context suppresses corrections the model registers internally, but under sustained multi-turn pressure hidden states drift toward a belief-flip boundary before the answer changes.
items.why: Shaky. Reported by 3 papers, all from 2026, and contested by P0403's account of gradual belief erosion.
items.note: The accounts may fit together, since P0403 studies extended multi-turn pressure while P3437 studies agreement within one exchange. P0487 finds its sycophancy direction overlaps little with a truthful direction, consistent with separate knowledge and deference.

items.title: Which inputs a steering arrow moves is still unpredictable
items.line: The same arrow moves some prompts and not others, and papers call predicting which ones an open problem.
items.status: 5 papers, 5 with a measured intervention

quote.text: steering effects are highly sample-specific: overall steerability trend is observable, but the outcome for an individual sample remains unpredictable

items.technical: Steering outcomes are sample-specific, with per-item success not predictable from the direction under the linear representation hypothesis, item-level variation collapsing under uniform steering, and the fitted rank-1 direction depending on the question as much as on prompt framing, while internal-signal diagnostics give only partial prediction.
items.why: Shaky. Named as unsolved by the papers themselves (P1327, P2355), and the five supporting papers are all 2026 and each proposes its own account.
items.note: P2355 predicts success from entropy and KL signals with an LLM judge as ground truth, and P1327 explains it by a sample-specific normal plane, so neither yet gives a tested way to say in advance which inputs will move.

items.title: Jailbreaks differ in whether they hide the harm
items.line: Some jailbreaks make a harmful request look harmless inside the model, while others leave the harm plainly visible and break refusal later.
items.status: 4 papers, 3 with a measured intervention, 2 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: position on refusal axis, 1 bare harmful and 0 benign rewrite
numbers.value: GCG 0.87 to 0.94, Simple 0.78 to 0.89, PAIR 0.23 to 0.36, Flip 0.08 to 0.28
numbers.where: surviving, entry A jailbroken prompt sits partway back

quote.text: safety-aligned LMs often represent Crescendo responses as more benign than harmful

items.technical: Multi-turn Crescendo moves representations toward the benign side (P3184) and research-role framing moves hidden states toward the non-refusal region (P0395), whereas a prefill attack leaves the harm reading at 0.91 to 0.98 while refusal collapses (P1799), different jailbreaks succeed through different intermediate concepts (P2376), and on our map a suffix attack (GCG) sits 0.87 to 0.94 of the way to the bare harmful request while rewriting attacks such as PAIR sit at 0.23 to 0.36.
items.why: Shaky. Each attack mechanism rests on one or two papers, and the papers differ on whether jailbreaks act on harm recognition or on the refusal step.
items.note: Our positions use P1216 groups, whose corpus build was flagged in the rebuild check (negatives are bare harmful prompts only), though the map axis here was fitted on sets sharing no texts with P1216. Scrambling attacks may simply stop the model recognising harm (striking_links.json). P3184 measures with a nonlinear MLP probe, not a direction. The survey site's map leaves the P1216 build out (RUNLOG 2026-09-26 10.34), and the rebuild check also found collapsed whitespace in ReNeLLM, CodeChameleon and some GPTFuzz prompts and special-token strings in 86 GCG prompts, so these positions are descriptive only.

items.title: Agent harm probes work in-domain but may count keywords
items.line: Probes flag harmful or hijacked agent states on their own benchmarks, but one study finds injection probes collapse once telltale words are removed.
items.status: 5 papers, 2 with a measured intervention, 3 with held-out accuracy, 2 against

numbers.label: P0395 refusal probe test accuracy
P3563 probe AUROC after lexical ablation, and on vocabulary-matched pairs

quote.text: the RepE-based circuit breaker successfully identifies and intercepts unauthorized actions before the agent commits to them

items.technical: Probes on agent hidden states separate harmful from benign coding-agent steps and carry to one-step lookahead (P1713), flag hijacked states under indirect prompt injection (P2968), decode refusal awareness at 89.19 percent test accuracy (P0395), privacy sensitivity out of distribution (P1300) and instruction authority (P3340). But standard probes trained on InjecAgent and AdvBench that reach AUROC 1.0 on AgentDojo fall below 0.10 once cue words such as ignore, bypass, system and instruction are removed (P3563), and a benign centroid fitted on another domain flags every InjecAgent run (P1347).
items.why: Shaky. Contested between papers, 5 reporting readable harm or hijack states (B yes in P1713, P2968 and P0395) and 1 showing that such probes can track surface words. We did not check whether any support paper runs a lexical control.
items.note: The steering results formerly here (P1713, P3335) moved to a separate solid finding, since lexical shortcuts in a probe do not undo a measured change in behaviour. P1713, P2968 and P1300 pick layers on evaluation data (our layer coding swept-test), P3340 does not say its accuracy is held out, and P2968 does not test its circuit breaker as an intervention. P3563 is a 2026 workshop paper coded refusal only, so outside the family by concept code. All five support papers are 2026, and three are preprints or workshop papers.

items.title: Probes beat output monitors, unless the text gives it away
items.line: Inner readers catch lies that answer checkers miss, yet they falter when the telltale words are removed or the model is trained to hide.
items.status: 5 papers, 1 with a measured intervention, 4 with held-out accuracy, 2 against

numbers.label: Probe recall after the CoT monitor has collapsed
Model organisms against unfiltered evaluation, Bias and Sandbagging AUROC

quote.text: While output monitors fail, we show that linear probes on internal activations can be used to reliably detect strategic dishonesty.

items.technical: Activation probes catch strategic dishonesty and obfuscated reward hacking that output or chain-of-thought monitors miss, detect motivated reasoning as well as or better than a CoT monitor and stay accurate on colluding agents told they are watched, but probe AUROC drops once textual evidence of the behaviour is filtered (0.57 against 0.94 on sandbagging model organisms) and fine-tuning can teach a model to evade unseen probes.
items.why: 5 supporting papers, 4 with B yes and 1 with C yes, across 6 coded model families. Shaky because contested between papers, 5 in favour and 2 whose results cut against it, all from 2025 to 2026.
items.note: P2966 finds telling agents about the monitor does not hide them (lines 30-31), which is prompting, while P3472 hides by fine-tuning, so the two are compatible. The P3451 figures here are from the full text, which differs from the abstract in papers.json (8 to 38 points there, 10 to 30 in the text).

items.title: Where the arrow is taken from changes whether it steers
items.line: Arrows built from the prompt's last token steer better than arrows built from finished answers, and the question used matters more than the wording.
items.status: 4 papers, 4 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy

quote.text: Prompt-only with last-token readout is strongest on average, while answer-only sources are weakest despite visibly exhibiting the target behavior.

items.technical: Prompt-only last-token activation sources give the strongest steering vectors and answer-only sources the weakest, and per-question variation dominates prompt-framing variation in rank-1 steering directions.
items.why: Shaky. The central results come from single 2026 papers (P2943, P2923) not yet replicated, with P0300 and P1861 giving related layer and token findings.
items.note: Our before-the-reply test fits this, since our two style and language links are already present at the last user token.

items.title: Whether reasoning moves through discrete phases is unsettled
items.line: Some papers read clear reasoning stages from the model's state, while one finds the process is smooth with no clean stages.
items.status: 4 papers, 3 with a measured intervention, 2 with held-out accuracy, 1 against

numbers.label: recovery of phase sequences by switching linear dynamical systems (NMI)

quote.text: mathematical reasoning traverses functionally ordered, step-specific subspaces

items.technical: Step identity, cognitive states and latent reasoning states are decodable and steerable (step-specific subspaces in P0270, a six-state machine in P1290, state clusters in P1829, step-level SAE features in P1321), while switching linear dynamical systems fail to recover keyword-marked phases and phase-discriminative directions are independent of top PCA directions (P3511).
items.why: Contested between papers, one negative result against four positive ones that use different methods and labels.
items.note: The full-text file for P3511 holds a different paper (a context-encoding method), so its claim is taken from its abstract and codes in SURVEY/data/papers.json and could not be quoted. The positive papers mostly label states with keywords, which P2559 finds unstable.

items.title: Robot action policies can be steered, but evidence is early
items.line: Directions inside vision-language-action robot models can change gripper, speed and height, but tests are small and the effect varies by model and task.
items.status: 4 papers, 4 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: P3464 effect sizes of fast vs slow clusters across 10 LIBERO-Long comparisons

quote.text: discrete robot actions can be steered by identifying a small number of meaningful features inside the residual stream of a VLA policy

items.technical: SAE-latent differences steer a Llama-3-based VLA's gripper action on one simulated task (P3215), FFN value-vector clusters steer speed and height in pi0 and OpenVLA in simulation and on a UR5 robot (P3464), closed-loop scaling of motion neurons improves the steering-success trade-off over static steering, which degrades success (P3356), and linear observers and controllers steer pi0.5 while OpenVLA's delta-yaw observation is not robust to linear perturbation (P3479).
items.why: Shaky. 4 workshop papers from 2025 and 2026, mostly one task or suite each, with limits in 3 of them and one near-zero effect called consistent (P3464).
items.note: The three against papers are also in support because they report the steering and its limit. The OpenReview abstract of P3479 in papers.json says OpenVLA action features are poorly linearly separable, but the full text on disk is the arXiv version, which says only that its delta-yaw observation is not robust, so we quote that. P3215 names only one task and one action pair. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P3356, P3464, P3479).

items.title: Reading what and when a model learned is patchy
items.line: Single papers read whether a text was in training, when a fact was learned, or memorised entries, with weak or domain-bound results.
items.status: 4 papers, 1 with a measured intervention, 3 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: Membership probe fitted on WikiMIA, read on ArxivMIA, AUC (P0150 Table 6)
numbers.where: line 1076 (Table 6 as extracted column by column, eval ArxivMIA, train WikiMIA, per lines 876-880)

numbers.label: Membership probe fitted and read on ArxivMIA, AUC (P0150 Table 6)
numbers.where: line 1077 (Table 6 as extracted column by column, eval ArxivMIA, train ArxivMIA)

quote.text: we show that linear probes can accurately (∼90%) distinguish “early” vs. “late” entities, generalizing to entities unseen during the probes’ own training.

items.technical: Logistic probes, CCS and mean-difference directions separate member from non-member texts, early from late fine-tuning stages (about 90%), real from fabricated memorised titles, and memorising from generalising behaviour, with held-out accuracy inside the fitting domain and steerable neuron shifts.
items.why: Shaky. Each quantity is read by one paper only (pre-training membership in P0150, fine-tuning order in a built setup in P1058, memorised catalogue entries in P2044, memorising against generalising neurons in P0591), membership on the harder ArxivMIA benchmark reaches only AUC 57.1 in-domain, and P2044 fails on numeric fields. Counts. 4 supporting papers, 3 with rubric B yes, 1 with rubric C yes, 6 open model families (API-only families not counted), 2 from 2026, 2 against or limiting.
items.note: Inside one domain only. P0150’s WikiMIA probe reads ArxivMIA near chance (and in-domain ArxivMIA itself reaches only 57.1, P0150.txt line 1077), and P2044 fails on numeric fields, both documented by the papers. P0591 steering is asymmetric and transfers poorly across tasks. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0150, P2044).

items.title: False facts meet wrong advice only on the plain ruler
items.line: On the plain cosine, false statements point with wrong advice and known entities against made-up ones, but the first link vanishes under the careful ruler.
items.status: exploratory, vanishes when whitened

numbers.where: P1063 by P0625 block median, recomputed by script

quote.text: a key part of these mechanisms is entity recognition, where the model detects if an entity is one it can recall facts about.

items.technical: Mined at Llama-3-8B-Instruct layer 16, the group-pair median cosine is -0.593 for Truth (P0163) against Misaligned advice (P1086) over 72 pairs, 0.551 for Factual recall (P1063) against Entity recall (P0957) over 60, and -0.410 for Factual recall against Confabulation (P0625) over 120, with whitened medians of -0.002, 0.054 and -0.029.

items.note: P0957 reports known against unknown entity directions within its own data; the cross-dataset knowledge link is ours and survived the checkers, but its pre-reply test (L4) was not scored. The scoop record lists the Valence-Assent Axis (arXiv 2510.27328) as a major overlap for the false facts with wrong advice link. Some counts here use the 72-dataset set from before four datasets were dropped on 2026-09-26.

items.title: Steering agents toward success gives small gains so far
items.line: Directions for task success or good procedure can nudge agents, but gains are small, match plain instructions, or are shown only in worked examples.
items.status: 3 papers, 2 with a measured intervention, 3 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: P3410 accuracy gain from steering toward success
P2418 average score for MiniCPM3-4B, base vs implicit steering

quote.text: This intervention yields a 1.1% accuracy boost

items.technical: Success-versus-failure probes are linearly separable in ScienceWorld and AlfWorld but steering along them adds 1.1 points against 6.8 for DPO (P3410), procedural steering vectors raise average scores over the base model (22.60 to 28.87 for MiniCPM3-4B) yet perform comparably to explicit textual instructions rather than better, while static CAA and Mass-Mean vectors struggle (P2418), and metacognitive steering of Kimi 2.6 is supported only by narrative trajectory comparisons (P2367).
items.why: Shaky. 3 papers with small, instruction-level or unquantified effects and no replication. P3410 uses one Llama-2 agent, P2367 one Kimi model, and P2418 two families (MiniCPM3 and Qwen3).
items.note: P3410 is a workshop paper and P2418 and P2367 are 2026 preprints. P2367 picks layers from alignment maps on the same rollouts (our layer coding).

items.title: Refusal may need several directions in larger models
items.line: Several papers find refusal spread over more than one arrow, and in larger Qwen3 models removing one arrow no longer stops it.
items.status: 4 papers, 4 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy, 1 against

quote.text: while ablating a single direction (𝑘 = 1) effectively suppresses refusal in smaller models, it proves insufficient for larger models (≥ 8B parameters)

items.technical: Gradient-optimized search finds multiple independent refusal directions and multi-dimensional concept cones (P1215), refusal categories map to geometrically distinct directions (P2800), false refusal spans several directions (P1087), and ablating one direction suppresses refusal in small Qwen3 models but not at 8B and above, where Qwen3 8B needs three directions to pass 50 percent attack success, whatever the extraction method (P3407). P2800 also finds that steering along any of these directions gives nearly the same behavior, and P2903 finds interchangeable circuits, so whether the extra directions matter for control is contested.
items.why: Shaky. Four family papers (2025 and 2026) over Qwen, Llama and Gemma, with held-out accuracy only in P3407, which is a short preprint tested on the Qwen3 family, and the behavioral weight of the extra directions is contested by P2800's one-knob result and P2903.
items.note: P3407 notes an unexplained MMLU drop on Qwen3 14B after ablation (lines 351-353). Most single-direction successes in the family use models of about 8B or smaller, so model scale may explain part of the disagreement, which no paper here tests directly. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P2800).

items.title: No single grammar arrow covers every phenomenon
items.line: Whether one grammar direction works for agreement, islands and quantifiers alike, or across languages, is disputed.
items.status: 4 papers, 1 with a measured intervention, 3 with held-out accuracy, 2 against

numbers.label: Within-phenomenon over cross-phenomenon accuracy gain (P2306, critical region)
Our held-out reading of BLiMP phenomena (P0260 rebuild), median over 12 phenomena
Same, weakest phenomenon (Quantifiers)
Agreement between the 12 phenomenon directions

quote.text: the probes that fit and test within the same phenomenon have a higher accuracy than its cross-phenomenon counterparts

items.technical: Grammaticality probes transfer across BLiMP phenomena at lower accuracy than within them, syntax change shares no common direction across languages, and our pooled difference of means reads held-out phenomena at about 0.7.
items.why: Shaky. Contested between papers, P2306, P1844 and P0365 against the broad generalization of P0260 and the shared features of P1378, and our supporting reading is measured at one setting only.
items.note: The second BLiMP rebuild (P2306 data) gives the same picture, weakest group 0.593. P0683 adds that ambiguity has no single direction. P1844 measures directions of historical change, a related but different quantity. P0365 finds minimal-pair differences align with fine linguistic categories but only weakly with broader ones.

items.title: Role and expert persona vectors help some tasks, hurt others
items.line: Adding a role such as economist to the model's state can raise scores in its own field but lower them in others.
items.status: 4 papers, 3 with a measured intervention

numbers.label: our re-measurement, weakest held-out occupational role under the pooled role direction
numbers.where: sets['Persona instructions, occupational roles'].loso_min and G

quote.text: improving in-domain task performance while also yielding unexpected crossdomain gains.

items.technical: Role vectors from persona prompts improve in-domain benchmark accuracy with unexpected cross-domain gains and losses, roles mainly change willingness to answer rather than knowledge, and expert persona vectors couple across domains unless decoupled.
items.why: Shaky. 4 papers with mixed per-domain results, and P0833 and P0753 code a weak group (G3 yes) and state the limit (G4 yes). P0841's record has placeholder codes, so its evidence is unchecked.
items.note: P0833 and P0753 appear in both lists because each reports gains and harms. The role signal itself is read well in our re-measurement, so the doubt is about what adding it does to tasks. P0753 finds boosting a confidence direction lowers factual accuracy. P0841's full text reports only gains from role steering (for example CSQA 31.86 to 39.80 percent on Llama3.1-8B, fulltext lines 27-28), so it supports the helping half only. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0753, P0833).

items.title: Whether image and text share one direction is contested
items.line: Vectors taken from text often steer image inputs, yet in CLIP-style models the same concept points different ways for images and text.
items.status: 4 papers, 4 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy, 4 against

numbers.label: P1224 gain of text-example task-vector patching over text-example prompting

quote.text: We find that VLMs align conceptually equivalent inputs into a shared task vector, which is invariant to modality (text, image) and format (examples, instruction)

items.technical: In generative VLMs, task and steering vectors derived from text transfer to image inputs (a text-example task vector patched onto image queries beats few-shot prompting by 14 to 33 percent in P1224, text-only backbone vectors raise spatial accuracy by up to 7.3 points in P0317, unsafe-text directions raise refusal on cross-modal inputs in P2845, and a text-prompt spurious vector corrects CLIP image embeddings in P0987), but SAE features for one concept in joint image-text embeddings are split by modality or point in different directions (P1071, P2635), and text-trained safety probes fail on image-text inputs (P0036).
items.why: Shaky. Contested between papers, 4 reporting transfer and 4 reporting that directions differ or fail across modality.
items.note: The two sides do not split cleanly by model type, since P0987 shows a text-prompt direction correcting CLIP image embeddings while P2635 and P1071 find modality-split SAE features in the same kind of model, so the conflict may be between estimators (a single prompt embedding versus SAE dictionaries) as much as between models. No family paper tests both on one model. P1606 builds a shared image-text concept set on purpose, which implies ordinary SAEs do not give one. P1604, a vision-language paper coded refusal only, adds that text-trained safety classifiers fall to about 60 percent on image inputs.

items.title: Pragmatic meaning has arrows, but perhaps not one each
items.line: Directions for implied meaning, rhetorical questions and metaphor can steer, yet different datasets give different rhetorical-question arrows.
items.status: 3 papers, 3 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy, 1 against

numbers.label: Agreement of the five scalar-diversity grade directions, our reading (P0230 data)
Weakest held-out grade, same

quote.text: uniform activation steering increases pragmatic interpretations globally but collapses item-level variation

items.technical: A single scalar-implicature direction shifts interpretation in four models and pragmatics change directions agree across languages, while rhetorical-question probes trained on different datasets rank items differently.
items.why: Shaky. Contested between papers (P0300 against a single direction), and each pragmatic phenomenon rests on one or two papers.
items.note: Our re-measurement supports one shared scalar-implicature direction across grades.

items.title: Label-free truth probes work but trail and mislead
items.line: Truth readers found without any labels beat plain prompting a little, but trail supervised readers and can latch onto the wrong feature.
items.status: 4 papers, 4 with held-out accuracy, 3 against

numbers.label: CCS gain over zero-shot, 6 models and 10 datasets
Unseen-topic accuracy, TTPD, LR, CCS, MM
CCS on MovieLens users and ratings files

quote.text: it outperforms zero-shot accuracy by 4% on average.

items.technical: Unsupervised contrast-pair probes (CCS, CRC and cluster-normalised variants) recover truth above zero-shot accuracy, but read held-out topics less accurately and less stably than supervised probes and can be misled by salient unrelated features.
items.why: 4 supporting papers, 4 with B yes and 0 with C yes, across 7 coded model families. Shaky because contested between papers, 4 report it working and 5 report it weaker, noisier or at chance on some data.
items.note: P0528 and P2044 appear on both sides, since each reports success on some data and failure on other data. P0896 transfer reads QNLI and PIQA near chance from most sources (g_coding). P1575 uses CCS only as a baseline. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0528, P2044).

items.title: What test awareness does to safety is unsettled
items.line: Steering test awareness changes safety behaviour by different amounts and in different directions across models, and one scaling claim rests on test-picked layers.
items.status: 2 papers, 1 with a measured intervention, 2 with held-out accuracy

quote.text: test awareness significantly impacts safety alignment (such as compliance with harmful requests and conforming to stereotypes) with effects varying in both magnitude and direction across models.

items.technical: Steering evaluation awareness shifts harmful compliance and stereotype conformity with a model-dependent sign (P1593), and the power law of awareness with model size (P3237) uses each model’s best layer by AUROC on the same evaluation set.
items.why: Shaky. Reported by only 2 papers, with opposite-signed effects across models and one single-paper scaling law on test-picked layers. Counts. 2 supporting papers, 2 with rubric B yes, 1 with rubric C yes, 5 open model families (API-only families not counted), 0 from 2026, 0 against or limiting.
items.note: Two papers, and the scaling law is a single workshop paper with layer choice coded swept-test in lt_coding.json.

items.title: Stereotype and pronoun choice share internal routes
items.line: The model seems to use the same internal features to pick gendered pronouns and to apply occupation stereotypes.
items.status: 2 papers, 2 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: cosine between occupational-bias and subject-pronoun feature vectors, one head path

quote.text: More surprising is that the feature vector for nbias for 6::6→9::1→... had a cosine similarity of 0.966 with the feature vector for nsubj for 6::6→9::1→13::11.

items.technical: Feature vectors for subject pronoun, object pronoun and occupational gender bias share heads with cosine up to 0.966, and causal subspaces for group binding and stereotype share one concept-level copying route.
items.why: Shaky, reported by only 2 papers, one on GPT-2 and GPT-Neo models and one on ten open models.
items.note: P1662 also finds no single mechanism explains pronoun behaviour, with three combined accounting for 91 to 99.5%. P1159's directions come from weights without data, so resampling stability does not apply.

items.title: Emotion and fairness arrows form at different training stages
items.line: A model becomes steerable for different emotions at different points in training, and trust-related concepts including fairness are readable early.
items.status: 2 papers, 2 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy

quote.text: linear steerability (i.e., the ability to adjust output via linear transformations of hidden states), emerges during intermediate stages of training

items.technical: Linear steerability for emotions emerges at intermediate training checkpoints, at distinct stages for anger and sadness, and trustworthiness concepts including fairness are linearly probeable early in pretraining.
items.why: Shaky, reported by only 2 papers on a few open checkpoint series.
items.note: Checkpoints are not groups in our rubric, so these results are outside the group analysis. P0848 reports seed means without spread (A no).

items.title: Whether an emotion makes a model safer is unsettled
items.line: Papers disagree on whether pushing an emotion makes a model safer or riskier, and the answer depends on the emotion, test and model.
items.status: 3 papers, 3 with a measured intervention, 1 against

quote.text: anger predictably elevates toxicity yet strengthens leakage resistance

items.technical: Reported safety effects of emotion steering differ in sign across emotions, metrics and models, from anger raising toxicity while strengthening leakage resistance to specific emotions improving safety, with no model-invariant mapping.
items.why: Shaky, contested between papers. 3 papers report safety effects of different sign and P2440 finds no stable mapping across models.
items.note: P0292 itself calls the effects idiosyncratic. The studies use different emotions, safety tests and models, so they do not strictly contradict each other, but nothing yet predicts the sign.

items.title: Different refusal arrows act as one knob
items.line: Refusal arrows found in different ways point in fairly different directions, yet pushing any of them changes refusal in much the same way.
items.status: 3 papers, 3 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy, 2 against

quote.text: activation steering along any refusal-related direction produces nearly identical refusal–over-refusal trade-offs, acting as a shared one-dimensional control knob

items.technical: Refusal directions for different categories (typical cosine 0.4 to 0.6) or from different estimators (difference of means, next-token and preference-optimized vectors, cosine 0.10 to 0.42) produce nearly identical refusal and over-refusal trade-offs (P2800) and use interchangeable circuits at the same layer (P2903), while P1215 finds gradient-optimized refusal directions that are representationally independent and argues that distinct mechanisms drive refusal.
items.why: Shaky. Contested between P2800 and P2903 on one side and P1215 on the other, and all three are 2025 or 2026 papers not yet replicated.
items.note: P2699 supports it indirectly, since a direction with no behavioral content matched only in size moves the same behaviors as real steers.

items.title: Steering out syllogism content bias works in some papers only
items.line: Some papers reduce the pull of believable content on logic judgments by steering, while others find steering barely helps.
items.status: 3 papers, 3 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy, 2 against

numbers.label: largest gain in formal reasoning accuracy from conditional kNN steering

quote.text: We show that both concepts are linearly represented and strongly aligned in representational geometry, leading models to conflate plausibility with validity.

items.technical: Validity and plausibility are linearly represented and aligned, and contrastive or debiasing vectors reduce content effects in some models (P0728, P0093, P0467), but static steering fails for some models (P0093) and two SemEval systems find activation steering limited and unable to separate logic from plausibility (P3067, P3121).
items.why: Contested between papers. Three report reduced content effects and two report steering that fails, on overlapping families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen).
items.note: P0093 needs conditional kNN steering to help unresponsive models, which is why it is on both sides. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0093).

items.title: One reasoning versus recall direction reads well but moves
items.line: A single direction separates reasoning questions from fact-recall questions, but after RL training it points somewhere quite different.
items.status: 2 papers, 1 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: cosine of the reasoning-recall mean direction before and after GRPO
AUROC of a one-dimensional projection separating the task groups

quote.text: identifying a set of linear features in the model’s residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall

items.technical: A difference-of-means direction between reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions separates them (AUROC 1.00 in Qwen3-0.6B) and steers accuracy in four base models, but after GRPO the direction's cosine to its earlier self averages 0.453 while decodability stays perfect.
items.why: Two papers only, and the second contests the stability the first relies on.
items.note: P1772 is a 2026 preprint on one small model and a 400-example set. P0681 shows null steering gains on some of its benchmarks. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P1772).

items.title: Task vectors transfer across datasets unevenly
items.line: Some visual task vectors carry from synthetic to real images or to unseen classes, but one trained on Asian questions fails on European ones.
items.status: 3 papers, 3 with a measured intervention, 2 against

numbers.label: P0377 M2IV trained on CVQA Asia, accuracy on Asia and on Europe

quote.text: We observe that the transferred function vectors achieve accuracy comparable to the original GQA-specific vectors across all relations

items.technical: Function vectors fit on synthetic images match GQA-specific vectors on real images (P1293), a task vector from source ImageNet classes compresses context for disjoint target classes at 64.2 against 65.0 percent for an oracle (P1324), and text-derived task vectors transfer to image queries (P1224), but an M2IV trained on the CVQA Asia split scores 60.11 on Asia and 32.15 on Europe (P0377), and MTV transfers only head locations while recomputing the vector on the target task (P1466).
items.why: Shaky. Contested between papers, 3 showing transfer and 1 showing a vector that does not carry, with a second paper transferring only head locations.
items.note: P0377 reports the Asia to Europe drop without comment but states elsewhere that M²IV seems to be task-specific and model-specific. P1460's averaged LIVE was removed from support because it includes both datasets in its fit, so it is not a held-out test (our group coding). P1466 reuses head locations and recomputes the vector on the target task, so it shows no failure, only that the vector itself was not tested for transfer. P1324's vector is used to compress context, not to steer.

items.title: A language arrow brings the language but not its knowledge
items.line: Steering toward a language changes the words, but it barely helps with the culture or facts tied to that language.
items.status: 2 papers, 2 with a measured intervention

numbers.label: Accuracy change on the held-out cultural scenarios set, per target language

quote.text: gains do not generalize uniformly across language-region pairs

items.technical: Language vectors from parallel corpora or target-language contrast pairs shift output language or answer distributions, yet leave culturally grounded accuracy flat or lower and trail persona prompting.
items.why: Shaky. Reported by only 2 papers, both 2026 workshop papers on Qwen or Gemma.
items.note: Both authors narrow their own claims, so this is an open problem rather than a failure hidden by a pooled score.

items.title: Truth transfer to low-resource languages is thinly tested
items.line: A truth arrow fitted in English seems to weaken in low-resource languages like Khmer, but only one truth paper shows it directly.
items.status: 2 papers, 1 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy, 1 against

numbers.label: English to Khmer probe transfer against in-distribution
SADI-HEAD with English pairs on XCOPA, Swahili, Tamil, Thai accuracy
Ours, truth by language, worst held-out language (Hindi)

quote.text: all languages provide the lowest transferability to Khmer, e.g., English→Khmer drops from 89% to 79% even in the most transferable layer.

items.technical: A knowledge-boundary direction fitted in one language transfers across languages but least well into low-resource Khmer, dropping from 89 to 79 percent English to Khmer in P0163, and English contrastive pairs leave Swahili, Tamil and Thai XCOPA near 50 percent in P1004, where the unsteered baseline is also near 50. P0819 instead finds value-concept transfer runs mostly from high- to low-resource languages.
items.why: 2 supporting papers, 1 with B yes and 1 with C yes, across 3 coded model families (Falcon, Llama, Qwen). Shaky because only P0163 shows it directly for a truth-like direction, P1004 is on XCOPA reasoning with a baseline already at chance, and P0819 reports a pattern that points the other way.
items.note: P0819 measures transfer as the gain over the target language's own accuracy and finds transfer from high- to low-resource languages more prevalent (lines 606-611), a different measure from P0163, so the two may not conflict directly. P1004 Table 10 columns are baseline, SFT, SADI-HEAD, SADI-NEURON (lines 1680-1700), and its baseline is already 50.20, 49.40 and 50.80 on Swahili, Tamil and Thai, so the chance readings are not a transfer drop. P1004 still writes that transfer is especially good in Tamil, Thai and Turkish (lines 1745-1746). P3075 is dropped, since it compares steering with persona prompting for shifting answers and does not test low-resource transfer. Our Hindi reading (0.730) is the worst held-out language in our reread of P0163.

items.title: Where the causal signal enters a VLM is unsettled
items.line: One paper finds last-token patching does nothing and image tokens carry the effect, another moves answers with a direction added at text tokens.
items.status: 1 paper, 1 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy, 1 against

numbers.label: P0390 share of outputs changed by full-sequence patching
P2242 delta-argmax for InternVL3-8B, object-word vs final-prefix-token injection

quote.text: The standard last-token interventions in LLM interpretability do not affect VLMs.

items.technical: P0390 reports that last-token activation patching, standard in LLM work, leaves VLM outputs unchanged, while full-sequence patching at MAC-identified layers alters 60 to 84 percent of outputs, with image tokens carrying almost all of the effect and text tokens none. P2242 instead adds a class-conditioned spatial direction at the object-word text token or at the final prefix token and moves answer logits, with the effect re-emerging at the final prefix token in deeper layers (InternVL3-8B prefix_last layer 20 delta-argmax +0.455). The two use different interventions, swapping whole activations from a counterfactual run versus adding a fitted direction, so the conflict may be about method rather than model.
items.why: Shaky. Contested between two 2026 papers, one finding that last-token and text-token interventions do nothing and one moving answers from exactly those positions.
items.note: The reader listed P2242 as support, but its interventions sit at text positions, obj_word and prefix_last (P2242.txt lines 286-289), so it cuts against the image-token claim. P1316 adds that visual conditioning acts sparsely across decoding steps, so averaging over a whole sequence dilutes the direction. P0390 picks its steering layer on the evaluation samples (our layer coding swept-test). The chain-of-thought result of P2242 is split into its own finding.

items.title: Models may know more about group opinions than they say
items.line: One paper finds a model's internal state predicts how different groups answer survey questions much better than its answers do.
items.status: 1 paper, 1 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy

numbers.label: improvement in alignment with human answer distributions, probe over outputs

quote.text: LLMs’ internal knowledge of opinions far exceeds what is revealed by their outputs, with a 52-66% improvement in alignment with the human answer distribution

items.technical: Linear probes on middle-layer activations predict demographic groups' opinion distributions with 52 to 66 percent better alignment than the model's outputs, a single probe over all groups does about as well as per-group probes, and steering attention-head SAE features shifts outputs toward chosen groups.
items.why: Shaky, reported by 1 paper (ICLR 2026) on Llama and Mistral.
items.note: The shared probe is trained on every group's questions, so each group is in-sample. P3500 finds a related preference vector shared across personas, with the evil persona the hardest to read. P1386 and P1034 steer toward group opinion distributions with separately fitted vectors.

items.title: Forgetting checked on outputs can leave knowledge readable
items.line: A model made to forget a skill or fact can still carry it inside, where a probe or a jailbreak brings it back.
items.status: 2 papers, 1 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy, 2 against

numbers.label: SAE-feature unlearning under four jailbreak formats, WMDP-Cyber accuracy

quote.text: linear probes trained on LMs’ representations can still perform tasks reliably after forgetting.

items.technical: After fine-tuning to forget, linear probes on hidden states still recover the forgotten task (P0374), and suppressing a few SAE features lowers WMDP-Cyber accuracy on standard prompts while jailbreak rewrites recover 33 to 42 percent against a 37.59 base (P0590), while subspace-projection and contrastive methods report robustness to aliases, paraphrases and recovery attacks.
items.why: 2 supporting papers, 1 with B yes and 1 with C yes, across 4 coded model families. Shaky because only 2 family papers show it and 3 report robust removal with other methods.
items.note: P0590 is on both sides, its own subspace method (SSPU) stays at or below 25 percent on all four jailbreak formats while the SAE-feature baseline recovers (g_coding). The 37.59 base accuracy is from the g_coding reading of P0590. P1282 and P1520 evaluate full unlearning methods, not a single direction. Papers listed both for and against in different families are kept as support (P0590).

items.title: Internal impressions rate African American English lower
items.line: A reader of the model's impressions scores tweets in African American English as less warm and less competent than mainstream English tweets.
items.status: 1 paper, 1 with held-out accuracy

quote.text: AAL tweets on average are associated with significantly lower warmth and competence scores than WME tweets.

items.technical: Warmth and competence probes fit on synthetic prompts assign significantly lower mean scores to African American Language tweets than to White Mainstream English tweets.
items.why: Shaky, reported by 1 paper, and the probes are validated only on synthetic data.
items.note: Our coding notes that the group difference in probe output is not a check of how well the probe reads each dialect, since there are no ground-truth labels per tweet. P0621, P1163 and P1646 use dialect as a race signal for steering but do not test this claim.

items.title: The model's self-knowledge may not be special
items.line: A probe on a different model predicts this model's mistakes about as well as a probe on its own insides, except for some factual questions.
items.status: 1 paper, 1 with held-out accuracy, 1 against

quote.text: On standard evaluation, we find no advantage: self-probes perform comparably to peer-model probes

items.technical: Correctness probes trained on a peer model's hidden states match self-probes on standard evaluation, with a self advantage appearing only on disagreement subsets of factual tasks and not on math.
items.why: Shaky because it is reported by only 1 paper and 1 paper points the other way.
items.note: Only one paper tests self against peer probes directly. P0406 argues probes capture a model-specific notion of difficulty distinct from human difficulty, which points the other way but without a peer-model control.

items.title: Whether one bias arrow serves every BBQ category is contested
items.line: Some results say one bias direction covers all social groups in the BBQ test, others find a direction that misses a category.
items.status: 1 paper, 1 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy, 3 against

numbers.label: our reading, P0663 BBQ contrast, worst held-out category (Religion)
our reading, P1856 BBQ contrast, Nationality pooled versus its own direction
numbers.where: sets['Cognitive bias, BBQ categories'] situation Nationality auroc_loso, auroc_within

quote.text: We find that the similarity between DSVs of different categories exceeds 0.90, suggesting that fairness-related features across these categories are similarly encoded in the model’s activation space.

items.technical: Per-category BBQ debiasing vectors have cosine above 0.90 and a pooled direction reads every held-out category at AUROC 0.994 or more, yet per-category classifiers transfer below 80% and a second BBQ contrast reads Nationality at 0.768.
items.why: Shaky, contested between papers and within P0663 itself; our two readings of the same BBQ corpus cut along the same eleven categories disagree on one category.
items.note: RUNLOG records that P0663 and P1856 are the same BBQ corpus with all eleven group names shared but almost no shared items, so the difference comes from the contrast each paper builds, not the categories. We had registered that the P0663 BBQ directions would fall below agreement 0.4 with a group below AUROC 0.6, and they did not (agreement 0.919 in loso_detection.json), so the pooled BBQ arrow is stronger than we expected. P1320 and P3295 find implicit (BBQ) and explicit (ToxiGen) bias directions entangled. Our readings are Llama-3-8B-Instruct layer 16.

items.title: Language distances in the model predict transfer only weakly
items.line: How far apart two languages sit inside a model is an unreliable guide to how well a skill carries from one to the other.
items.status: 1 paper

quote.text: We find that each distance metric either only moderately correlates or does not correlate with crosslingual transfer performance, and metrics do not generalize well across models, layers, and tasks.

items.technical: Centroid, subspace and language-separability distances between language representations correlate only moderately or not at all with zero-shot cross-lingual POS and NER transfer in three multilingual encoders and do not generalize across models, layers and tasks, though pairwise separability is a reasonable predictor.
items.why: Shaky. Reported by 1 paper, on encoder models only (BERT-family).
items.note: It sits beside the solid finding that language arrows group by family. Languages can cluster sensibly and still not tell you how well transfer will go. Our re-measurement does not test this.

items.title: Persona directions often survive rewording, with notable exceptions
items.line: Some persona directions stay the same when instructions are reworded, while others change direction with how the prompt is built.
items.status: 2 papers, 1 with a measured intervention, 3 against

numbers.label: our re-measurement, evil and impolite persona wordings, weakest held-out wording
numbers.where: sets['Persona, evil, wordings'] and ['Persona, impolite, wordings'].loso_min

numbers.label: our re-measurement, P1436 prompt framings, weakest held-out framing and framings below 0.6
numbers.where: sets['Persona trait, prompt framings'].loso_min and n_below_060

quote.text: We observe IntraCos(i) ≫ InterCos(i, j), which means directions for the same persona are highly consistent across prompt variants

items.technical: Persona vectors refit on paraphrased prompts or other contrast baselines can be near-identical, yet CAA vectors of the same behaviour built from different prompt constructions often point differently, and vectors fitted in one prompt setting generalise poorly to others.
items.why: Shaky, contested between papers and between our own datasets. P0757 and P1338 find high stability across rewordings, while P3308, P1436 and P2923 find prompt construction changes the direction or its reach.
items.note: In our re-measurement the BASE, SYS-NEG and USER-NEG framings of the P1436 data are weakly separable even on their own (own-group AUROC 0.549, 0.63 and 0.58 in loso_detection.json situations), so part of the failure is a weak signal in those framings, not only transfer. P2923 finds per-question effects explain more of a direction's variation than prompt framing.

items.title: Is a plain mean difference enough for this concept
items.line: Some papers find the simple average-difference direction as good as trained classifiers, while others beat it with whitening or nonlinear methods.
items.status: 2 papers, 2 with a measured intervention, 2 with held-out accuracy, 9 against

quote.text: That centroid distance matches probe performance indicates class separation is a mean shift

items.technical: Difference-of-means directions match trained probes (centroid distance within 0.02 AUC of logistic probes) and generalise better in some papers, while whitened Fisher discriminants, nonlinear lifts and context-dependent fields outperform them in others.
items.why: Shaky because it is contested, 2 papers support it and 9 limit or contradict it.
items.note: The comparisons use different baselines and uses (reading against steering), so they do not test one question. The within 0.02 figure is P3560's own (runs/soundness/survey_search/fulltext/txt/P3560.txt line 417). SteeringSafety (P3295 and its later version P1320) finds DIM and ACE strongest for harm and bias, but for hallucination PCA and LAT win on Llama and Qwen and only conditional DIM helps on Gemma (P3295.txt lines 301-308).

items.technical: 21 of 66 source-defined datasets hold a group whose leave-one-group-out AUROC is below 0.7 (79 of 850 groups in 23 of 68 datasets overall), and 16 of those 23 datasets have an item-level split-half stability of 0.9 or more.
items.why: Problematic, one pooled score hiding a group read poorly, shown on 21 source-defined datasets by direct count; P2546 and P0486 report the same pattern in their own tables.
items.note: Counts recomputed without the four dropped datasets. These are point readings, and a small group can fall below 0.7 by chance. Our reading is mostly not the authors' own model and layer. P1509's Stakes dataset has its worst group at 0.663 at our reading, and the rebuild check found that build faithful. Pooled five-fold held-out accuracy does warn when a group is read backwards (see the added finding), so the hiding is sharpest for weak, not reversed, groups. Merged from 4 verified findings across cross-cutting, emotion-bias, truth-honesty, style-language (ours06, emot11, trut25, styl05).

items.technical: Registered coding of 881 papers (kappa 0.879 for the layer code) finds the main layer chosen on the evaluation data in 235 papers (26.6 percent weighted) against 169 on held-out data (18.0 percent), no single practice above 27 percent, the token not stated in 144 papers (17.1 percent), and main-layer depth quartiles of 0.47 to 0.81, which overlap the 0.31 to 0.7 band where truth geometry flipped in our depth sweep.

quote.text: the association between the source-fitted score and target truthfulness can reverse across datasets, rather than simply becoming weaker.

Cross-architecture mapped misalignment directions give large effects that random directions match (P1696), and steering along a random direction raises harmful compliance from 0 to between 1 and 13 percent (P3568), while other papers find norm-matched random directions give no similar effect (P1746, P1898).
items.why: A paper's own control shows its measured effect is not specific to the concept (P1696), and random pushes alone move a safety output (P3568), so a C yes without a random control can mislead. Only two papers show it, so the size of the problem is unknown.
items.note: All four papers are 2026 and C yes in papers.json, over Llama, Qwen, Gemma and Falcon. P1696's failure is for directions mapped across architectures, not its within-model directions. The 127 is a keyword count that includes papers merely mentioning random vectors, so it is only a loose upper bound on papers running a random control, and the rubric does not code the control. In plain words, if shoving the model in any direction changes its answers, a shove along the concept arrow changing them does not show the arrow is the concept.

items.technical: A monolithic privacy direction fitted on synthetic data raised CONFAIDE leakage from 24.1% to 47.4% on Llama-3.1 and reads CONFAIDE Tier 2 at AUROC 0.43, and a mass-mean privacy vector moved SALAD and Confaide the wrong way on Llama-2-13b-chat while P0118 reports gains in most tasks.
items.why: Problematic. One pooled direction reverses on held-out benchmarks, and a pooled summary hides tasks that move the wrong way. Counts. 2 supporting papers, 2 with rubric B yes, 2 with rubric C yes, 4 open model families (API-only families not counted), 2 from 2026, 1 against or limiting.
items.note: P0397 qualifies its claim and moves to per-parameter axes. P0118 does not, and its table extraction is garbled, so the per-task reading comes from our G coding. P1300 finds a linear privacy probe holds on PrivacyLens, a read-only use rather than steering.

items.title: Sycophancy directions also suppress agreeing with the truth
items.line: Turning down a sycophancy direction can also make the model agree less with true statements and update less on real evidence.
items.status: 3 papers, 3 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy, 2 against

numbers.label: mean reduction in agreement, sycophantic items against hard-fact correct-stance items

quote.text: The direction accordingly reduces agreement with factually correct statements (e.g. that the Earth is round) as well as sycophantic ones.

items.technical: A centroid-difference sycophancy direction projects equally onto sycophantic and factually correct agreement and reduces both, yielding-under-pressure and rational-updating directions are positively aligned, and fixed-direction anti-sycophancy steering trades resisting pressure against updating on evidence.
items.why: Problematic, a direction tracking a proxy (agreement in general rather than sycophancy). Shown by 3 papers with measured interventions on Llama, Gemma, Qwen and Mistral, while P3437 and P0487 find the deference signal separable from knowledge, so the size is contested.
items.note: P2001 tests one model and still finds hard-fact agreement falls far less than sycophantic agreement (14.3 against 88.9 percent), so the direction is weakly selective, not blind. All 3 support papers are from 2026.

items.title: One readout at the last prompt token misses wrapped requests
items.line: Reading only the last position before the reply can miss harmful requests hidden inside jailbreak wrappers, even when the harmful signal appeared earlier.
items.status: 3 papers, 1 with a measured intervention, 3 with held-out accuracy, 2 against

numbers.label: P1759 detection, clean held-out against wrapped, three models

quote.text: The probes retain high recall on clean held-out SorryBench harmful prompts, but miss a substantial fraction of the same harmful requests once they are wrapped in HarmBench jailbreak templates

items.technical: Final-token or terminal readouts of harmfulness lose recall on template-wrapped or restructured inputs, and the harm signal is visible at earlier positions, for example at the end of the user's instruction rather than the last template token.
items.why: A readout practice that three family papers show loses the harm signal on restructured inputs, over Llama, Mistral, OLMo and Qwen.
items.note: Depends on the input kind. P0533's last-token direction gate kept jailbreak-template attacks near zero in its setting, and P1545 finds final-token probes useful for predicting a model's own failures. P1542 supports only the earlier-position part.

items.title: Models trained against probes can slip past them
items.line: When a model is trained to fool an activation monitor, it can learn to hide the signal the monitor reads.
items.status: 3 papers, 3 with held-out accuracy, 2 against

quote.text: our attacks can often reduce recall from 100% to 0% while retaining a 90% jailbreaking rate.

items.technical: Three papers show latent-space monitors failing under optimisation pressure, with fine-tuned models evading unseen probes zero-shot (P3472), RL-trained models evading token-level monitors and generalising to unseen ones (P3282), and obfuscation attacks cutting harmfulness-probe recall from 100 to 0 percent at a 90 percent jailbreak rate (P3708).
items.why: Solid by the literature rule. Three separate papers report it, all with held-out accuracy (rubric B yes in papers.json), each over at least two model families (P3472 Gemma, Llama, Qwen and an API model, P3282 Llama and Qwen, P3708 Gemma and Llama), and the limits found are stated by the papers themselves.
items.note: Which monitors resist is contested. P3282 finds max-pooling and attention probes robust to its attack and P3472 finds ensembles partly resist, while P3708 reports probes, SAEs and OOD detectors all vulnerable to its attacks and that obfuscation costs performance on a complex task. P3708 is a recall addition outside the open-problems extraction. I did not search the whole corpus for a paper where evasion fails, so the no-unqualified-counterexample condition rests on the papers read here. Two papers limit the claim to optimisation against the probe itself. Telling agents they are monitored does not hide them from probes (P2966), and probes keep high recall when a model learns to fool a chain-of-thought monitor rather than the probe (P3600). Merged from 3 verified findings across cross-cutting, refusal-safety, style-language (open22, rmon11, styl34). The family readers placed these under new, problematic, solid; the editor placed the merged item under problematic.

items.title: Harm arrows fade in low-resource languages
items.line: A harm or refusal arrow built mostly from big languages reads Yoruba and Chichewa much worse, and English control is weaker in Catalan and Hungarian.
items.status: 2 papers, 2 with a measured intervention, 1 with held-out accuracy, 1 against

numbers.label: held-out AUROC of Yoruba, Refusal languages (PolyRefuse)
held-out AUROC of Chichewa, Harmfulness languages (P0819 rebuild)
P0819 En-Control following rate, LLaMA2-chat-70B
held-out AUROC of Catalan and Hungarian, Harmfulness languages (P0819 rebuild)

quote.text: unidirectional cross-lingual transfer between high- and low-resource languages

items.technical: Refusal and harm directions pooled over languages or fitted in English transfer well to most languages but read or steer some much worse. English control of harmful following on LLaMA2-chat-70B is 63.11 in Catalan and Hungarian against 95.15 in French (P0819), the English misalignment direction is negligible for Marathi (P3375), and in our re-readings a held-out AUROC is 0.712 for Yoruba against a median of 0.996 over 14 PolyRefuse languages and 0.805 for Chichewa in P0819's own data, where Catalan and Hungarian read at 0.987 and 0.992.
items.why: Problematic. A transfer failure documented by two family papers and our measured corpus reading, where a pooled score over languages hides one weak group. P0819 calls English control comparable and does not restrict the claim for Catalan and Hungarian (g_coding G4 no).
items.note: PolyRefuse is not a family paper, and its Yoruba reading falsified a main-text claim of our survey (HANDOFF.md). On our directions map Yoruba sits at 0.196 against the pooled arditi_src direction, and how often a language's harmful items retrieve their English translation tracks this cosine at Spearman 0.96 (striking_links.json), which points to the model reading the language poorly rather than to a different harm concept. P3330 finds strong English and Chinese transfer, both high-resource. P3375 reports its English misalignment direction as strongly shared for Yoruba, so Yoruba's weak reading here is specific to the refusal direction on this model.

items.title: Emotion steering can fail or flip on some tasks
items.line: The same emotion push that works on average can do nothing or the opposite on some decision games or a smaller model.
items.status: 2 papers, 2 with a measured intervention, 2 against

quote.text: This is clearest in the Escalation Game, where several models show weak or negative alignment

items.technical: Papers document emotion directions whose effect is near zero or reversed on particular decision games or model sizes while the pooled effect is positive.
items.why: Problematic, a transfer failure the papers document themselves. 2 papers show a task or model where the push fails or reverses.
items.note: P2440 reports near-zero or negative alignment in the Escalation Game for Qwen2.5-0.5B and InternVL3-1B (lines 1440 to 1442 of its full text). P2862 uses a 4-prompt probe, so its reversal is small evidence. P2178 and P0325 report the same direction holding on every added dataset they tried, so failure is not universal. P1561 (joy steering whose effect varies between comedy and horror reviews) and P0600 (held-out sentiment gain smaller but still positive, 20.2 to 37.8 per g_coding.json) were removed from support, since neither shows a near-zero or reversed effect; they show a weaker group.

items.title: Function and task vectors fail on most new models
items.line: When one group tried these vectors on 36 models, most model and task pairs did not get their few-shot accuracy back.
items.status: 1 paper, 1 with a measured intervention, 4 against

numbers.label: model-task combinations where default function vectors recover 5-shot performance
the same after searching heads and scale
model-task combinations recovered by task vectors

quote.text: FVs with default parameters recover 5-shot performance in only 20% of model-task combinations, and 52% with parameter search across An and λ; TVs perform poorly as well at 35%.

items.technical: Across up to 36 models from 14 families, function vectors with default settings recover 5-shot performance in 20 percent of model-task combinations (52 percent after hyperparameter search) and task vectors in 35 percent, with many models showing no gain or a loss, so results first shown on GPT-J and a few Llama models do not generalise.
items.why: A transfer failure a paper documents at scale (one paper, 36 models, 14 families). It limits every family paper that reports these vectors on a handful of models.
items.note: Other papers report working vectors on Llama, Gemma, Mistral, OLMo and Qwen models (P3539, P1512, P3100, P0769), so the failure is uneven rather than universal. P0204 also finds that the heads behind a function vector differ by model.

items.title: Alignment training hides value directions instead of removing them

quote.text: alignment training does not remove the structured partisan direction in the base model.

items.technical: Post-training leaves value-laden directions in place while cutting or reshaping their route to output, for example a partisan direction persisting in Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with policy features silenced, a shared sycophancy and lying head circuit persisting after an RLHF refresh cut sycophancy tenfold, and cultural distinctions encoded more sharply after alignment.
items.why: New. 2025 and 2026 papers on Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral and Phi each report a version of it, but each tests a different value and mostly one base and instruct pair, so it is not yet replicated as one claim.
items.note: The direction of the change differs by paper. P0611 finds the ethics and culture discordance larger in instruct models, P2794 finds post-training pushes sycophantic lying away from other truth types, and P3577 finds psychometric structure only in instruct models.
